hits.title: A closer look at “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming”
hits.body:
GPT-6 Astra’s improvement of Qwen’s math is not “native weight editing” but activation steering with clever use of synthetic data

Zhi Wang, Brandon Hsu, Tianhao Wang, Mikhail Belkin (UC San Diego). Code: GitHub.


TL;DR

 * Astra’s edit of Qwen is equivalent to a special case of context-dependent activation steering: it pushes the activations along a fixed direction constructed from data, with a strength that depends linearly on the current activations.
 * Generalizing Astra’s edit, with a trained “sensing vector” that determines how strongly to push along the same fixed direction, can further improve the effectiveness of the edit.
 * Astra constructs the fixed direction from short synthetic traces rather than from Qwen’s real rollouts, a design choice that turns out to be substantially more effective.

In a widely circulated blog post Sparks of Weight-Space Programming, the authors highlight how GPT-6 Astra edits a small language model without any training: it writes a short program that changes parts of the MLP weight matrices to significantly improve the math performance of the model. The authors present this as evidence for a new paradigm they call Weight-Space Programming, stating that “neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights.” They even frame this as a shift away from symbolic optimizers like Adam, which has been the default optimizer for training deep learning models since its introduction in 2014. The post, and especially its claim that frontier LLMs like Astra can “natively” edit weights, has received considerable attention. A single tweet by the lead author has been viewed nearly 10 million times (as of November 2026). While the authors and many commentators interpret Astra’s edit as “native weight editing,” we argue that Astra is acting like a clever researcher, effectively implementing existing activation steering techniques combined with synthetic data. Additionally, recognizing the edit as activation steering allows us to further improve on Astra’s approach.


1. From “native weight editing” to activation steering

Background: Astra’s approach to improving Qwen3.5-0.8B at math. Astra is prompted to improve the math performance of Qwen3.5-0.8B. The prompt explicitly mentions looping as a possible issue but does not say how to fix it. After some exploration, Astra settles on an approach. Here is a summary of the key steps. Astra first inspects Qwen’s rollouts and confirms that looping is a critical issue. It then generates a dataset of short synthetic pairs, with and without repetition, and uses it to build a direction that isolates looping. It identifies key locations in the model to steer and applies to the MLP output weight matrices at those locations.

At a high level, this procedure follows a standard recipe from the activation steering literature. In particular, we show that Astra’s edit of Qwen3.5-0.8B is a special case of a known form of context-dependent activation steering, and that in some settings this view lets us improve on it.

There is already a discussion of how to understand “native weight editing” as described in the original blog post, including critical takes on its interpretation. See, for example, Matthew Honnibal’s post, Sean Goedecke’s commentary, and crabbix’s LessWrong post. Here we provide a formulation of the algorithm, experiments decoupling sensing (how much to push) from the steering direction (which way to push), and an examination of Astra’s use of synthetic data.[1]


Formulation: activation steering

Qwen, like most LLMs, is built from a stack of transformer blocks. Take any one of these blocks, and let the MLP’s hidden activations right before the output matrix be , its output weight matrix be , the residual stream be , and this MLP’s contribution to the residual stream be . Steering is the process of adding a vector to , , or to elicit certain behaviors from the model. Consider the steered activation vector







There are two vectors here:

 * The steering direction says where to push.
 * The sensing vector determines the steering strength through the inner product , where the activation provides the context.

Here the strength depends on the output of the MLP. Because the strength is linear, this intervention is the same as a weight edit to the MLP output weight matrix (assuming no bias):







In this framing, Astra's edit on Qwen picks . In general, one is free to design both and ; in this post we focus on training , which further reduces looping.

Figure 1. The two dashed paths compute the same output: weight editing gives (purple), while activation steering gives (green).

We call this formulation context-dependent activation steering, not to be confused with another form of steering which does , where is a fixed number and context independent. The terminology is based on Contextual Linear Activation Steering (CLAS), Hsu et al., 2026, which trains a sensing vector.[2]


2. Qwen’s poor math performance in the original setup is pathological

The headline claim is that Astra edits Qwen3.5-0.8B to make it better at math. What the edit actually does is suppress looping when thinking mode is turned on, which in turn raises Qwen’s math scores. Admittedly, the original blog post mentions this but underemphasizes it.

We reproduce the experiment in Qwen3.5-0.8B’s thinking mode under the blog setting. Here “Astra’s steering” means , with built from Astra’s four synthetic pairs.[3]

Throughout this post, a loop means a 30-token sequence appearing at least 20 times. A trace is said to loop if it contains at least one loop. Loop rate is the fraction of traces that loop. Cap hit means reaching the token limit.[4]

Our evaluation uses the same problems as the original blog: 576 GSM8K training problems and 576 MATH training problems.

3. Training the sensing vector can improve on Astra’s steering

Here, the goal of steering is to reduce the loop rate. Accuracy, thinking closure, and cap hits are tracked as secondary metrics and are not directly optimized. We show that training sensing vectors can further reduce looping compared to Astra’s steering approach.

Astra’s steering approach in the original blog sets . It uses the same direction both to sense the context and to steer. To improve on this approach, we keep the direction to steer the same but use rather than to sense. We compare Corrective next-token prediction (Corrective NTP) and Unlikelihood (UL) for training .

Specifically, let be the steered model and the original model. Also let positive () denote non-loop text (called “productive” in the original blog) and negative () denote loop text. We define the corrective next-token prediction loss, the unlikelihood loss, and the KL divergence as follows:







Here averages over positive continuation tokens following loop prefixes; averages over the original positive tokens for KL; averages over loop tokens from the second copy of the repeated chunk onward. We average tokens within each trace, then average across pairs. Only is optimized, model weights are frozen.

Based on these, we consider the following methods:

Method

Training data and signal for

Objective

Corrective NTP

Increase likelihood of positive continuations after loop prefixes



Unlikelihood

Decrease likelihood of repeated tokens in negative traces





No sensing vector training; choose on development data

—

We use either Astra’s four original pairs or those four plus 28 additional hand-written pairs. Each pair consists of two rollouts, one is positive, the other negative (containing loops). These underlying pairs are used to construct and used to supply the training text to learn . Unlikelihood uses the negative traces. Corrective NTP places the positive continuation after varying amounts of repetition from its paired negative text.

For example, one of Astra’s four pairs shares this prompt and opening:

> Prompt: A machine makes 45 necklaces, and another makes 2.4 times as many. Find the total.
> 
> Shared opening: The second machine makes 45*2.4=108 necklaces. Add the first machine's 45 to obtain 153 necklaces.

The two continuations are:

> Positive: Multiplication gives the second quantity, while addition combines the two machines. A check is 45*3.4=153.
> 
> Loop: Is 108 the total? No, 45+108=153. Is 108 the total? No, 45+108=153. Is 108 the total? No, 45+108=153.

For Corrective NTP, we put copies of the loop chunk before the positive continuation and apply the next-token loss only to the positive tokens. After the same shared opening, one example is:[5]

> Loop prefix: Is 108 the total? No, 45+108=153. Is 108 the total? No, 45+108=153.
> 
> Positive continuation: Multiplication gives the second quantity, while addition combines the two machines. A check is 45*3.4=153.

At each steered layer, is the difference between the mean residual stream over the last 36 tokens of the negative text and that of the positive text, averaged over pairs and normalized to unit length. For (Astra's method) we sweep . Sensing vector training uses Adam with early stopping. Development data select hyper-parameters and early stop step.


Result: less looping with trained sensing vector

Figure 2a. Qwen3.5-0.8B on 576 GSM8K problems. Differences versus the original model (left) and Astra’s steering (, matched pair count; right), in percentage points or tokens (k = thousands). Green: improvement; red: deterioration. All cells use paired bootstrap estimates; stars mark 95% intervals that exclude zero.

Figure 2b. Qwen3.5-0.8B on MATH, 576 test problems. Comparisons, colors and stars follow Figure 2a.

Figures 2a and 2b show each dataset separately. Figure 2c pools GSM8K and MATH, 1,152 test problems in total.

Figure 2c. Pooled GSM8K and MATH results, including the original thinking-on model (gray). Lower loop rate is better; higher accuracy is better. Bars show the observed percentages. Astra’s steering () uses at both pair counts.

With 32 pairs, Unlikelihood training reduces the loop rate from 27.2% with to 6.5%; Corrective NTP reduces it to 10.9%. At four pairs, the corresponding loop rates are 29.5%, 11.1% and 15.7%. Training can do the intended job of fixing this pathological behavior better.


4. A non-pathological setting shows loop reduction with similar accuracy

We show that steering can reduce looping in a non-pathological setting, though with smaller side effects on accuracy.

We also test Qwen3-1.7B under greedy decoding, steering at blocks 15–18, on 500 MATH level-5 and 500 LiveCodeBench prompts. Unlike the Astra setting, thinking here is worth a great deal: turning it off costs 26.4 accuracy points. Here are some observations:[6]

 * either or a trained sensing vector can reduce looping more than thinking off.
 * Training the sensing vector can further reduce loop rates and generated token counts on average compared with .

The pairs for training and building are math-style text, yet the steering also helps suppress loops on code, loop suppression seems to transfer with these directions.

Figure 3a. Qwen3-1.7B on 500 MATH level-5 prompts, greedy decoding. Cells show differences versus the original model with thinking on, in percentage points or completion tokens (k = thousands). Green indicates improvement; red, deterioration. All cells use paired bootstrap estimates; stars mark 95% intervals that exclude zero. Accuracy colors saturate at ±8 points.

Figure 3b. Qwen3-1.7B on 500 LiveCodeBench prompts, greedy decoding. Comparisons, colors and stars follow Figure 3a. Both benchmarks use math-style steering pairs.


5. Where do steering vectors come from and where to sense?


Astra's short synthetic pairs are especially effective for steering direction

We compare steering directions constructed from short synthetic pairs with those constructed from the unedited model’s own looping and non-looping responses, using the Qwen3-1.7B setting of Section 4. For the natural traces, we retain the preceding response as context but use short windows of looping or non-looping text to construct and train . We test both and an Unlikelihood-trained .[7]

Figure 4. Qwen3-1.7B, 500 prompts per dataset. Changes from the original model with 95% intervals. Circles: short synthetic pairs; diamonds: natural traces. Blue: Astra’s steering; green: Unlikelihood-trained . Lower loop rate is better; higher accuracy is better. The dashed vertical line at zero marks no change from the original model.

Overall, short synthetic pairs give much stronger loop reduction while accuracy stays roughly the same, supporting Astra’s choice of synthetic pairs for constructing the steering direction. Our tentative explanation: long responses differ in content, position and reasoning path as well as looping, adding unrelated variation to the activation contrast. Short synthetic pairs may isolate repetition more cleanly.


Where to sense: MLP output or residual stream?

We find that a trained sensing vector transfers directly to residual-stream sensing, whereas Astra’s method needs its strength recalibrated.

There are three sites worth distinguishing: MLP hidden activations before output , the MLP output , and the residual stream . Even when two interventions use the same and ,







sense different quantities. The second sensing sees the accumulated stream: the embedding, every earlier attention and MLP output, and the corrections made by earlier steering interventions.[8]

We moved these two steering methods from the MLP output to the residual stream in the Astra setup, keeping and unchanged. We also recalibrated for the residual stream with , chosen on the development problems like every other setting. Development accuracy was 39.8%, 66.0%, 66.0% and 63.7%; of the two tied settings, loops less (3.5% against 12.5%) and was chosen. On the 1,152 test problems:

Figure 5. Pooled GSM8K and MATH results, 1,152 test problems. Blue: ; green: unlikelihood-trained . Residual uses the recalibrated strength. Bars show observed percentages.

The sensing vector trained on the MLP output transfers to the residual stream with a similar benefit. The method needs retuned. Recalibrated to , it gives a similar benefit to the MLP-output steering methods: about the same accuracy, with loop rates as low as the trained sensing vector's.


6. Conclusion

Astra’s weight edit can be understood as context-dependent activation steering. This view separates where to push from how strongly to push, and training the sensing vector can further reduce looping. The data used to construct the direction and train the sensing vector, and the site where it senses, all matter. Astra’s short synthetic pairs are a particularly effective choice in our comparison.

In short, we find that Astra is a clever researcher who can troubleshoot issues independently: it may not find the best solution, but it can provide useful insights, such as constructing the steering direction from synthetic data rather than real outputs.

----------------------------------------


7. Notes

Reproduction details. The GitHub repository contains the code and experiment recipes. The supplement gives the protocols, including how we selected the Qwen3 test prompts; those prompts include known looping cases, so their loop rates are not benchmark-wide estimates.

Positive-only NTP. Training on the original positive traces alone does not work well for suppressing loops. Its method and results are in the supplement.

Design choices for steering. Astra’s short pairs and simple are effective choices. Which data to use to construct and train , where to sense, and what behavior the objective preserves are all consequential design choices. This also suggests a constructive role for agents: searching this design space, inspecting failures, and trying different training objectives and train/dev sets.

Steering across temperatures. Switching the Astra setup to greedy decoding without retuning sharply reduced development accuracy. Removing only the presence penalty had a smaller effect. The and that work under one temperature may need retuning under another; the decoding diagnostic gives the comparison.

Another axis: how to construct the steering direction. We focused on , but is another vector to construct from data. A natural next comparison is to try mean differences of residuals, logistic regression, recursive feature machines, and PCA while keeping the sensing vector fixed.

Training the sensing vector has dataset-specific side effects. On GSM8K, the completion metrics move in the favorable direction numerically. On MATH, exact repetition falls dramatically, but more answers exhaust the budget and fewer close thinking. Some capped responses paraphrase instead of repeating exactly. The dataset-level diagnostics show the breakdown.

Neuron selection in Astra’s final steering. Astra later restricted steering to 64 MLP neurons per layer. This version reaches 60.2% accuracy and a 29.6% loop rate, compared with 57.7% and 29.5% for our earlier four-pair baseline. It senses selected hidden neurons rather than their combined MLP output. The supplement gives its equivalent formulation and separate random-direction control.

When to early stop sensing vector training? We need a validation criterion, but what should it measure? Teacher forcing on saved development traces is cheap; generating fresh rollouts measures the accuracy, repetition, and completion we actually care about, but is much more expensive. Falling training loss did not reliably preserve thinking closure in our runs. The early-stopping diagnostic describes the proxies we tried and the closure check we used.

 1. ^
    
    Neuron selection. Our baseline uses Astra’s steering method. Note that a later variant by Astra selects 64 neurons per layer for steering; see the discussion below.

 2. ^
    
    Literature attribution. The connection between activation and weight edits was established in Arditi et al., 2024 (weight orthogonalization being equivalent to directional ablation under certain conditions). Other relevant work includes Meng et al., 2022, Zou et al., 2023, and Wu et al., 2024.

 3. ^
    
    Setup. For the specific setup, see reproduction details.

 4. ^
    
    Token limits. The Qwen3.5-0.8B limit counts generated tokens only; the Qwen3-1.7B limit includes the prompt. Exact budgets are in the supplementary methods.

 5. ^
    
    Corrective data. The construction details describe how we vary the number of copies for each pair.

 6. ^
    
    Setup. For the specific setup, see reproduction details.

 7. ^
    
    Setup. See the supplementary methods for trace construction and selection and stopping rules.

 8. ^
    
    Sensing location. This changes what the same does. Take with unit . At the output, each steering intervention multiplies the sensed coordinate of its own MLP's output by , once, and leaves the rest of the stream alone. On the residual stream, each intervention acts on the accumulated stream. For an existing residual contribution, the direct effect of two steering interventions is . If both use the same unit direction , its coordinate along is multiplied by . With different layer-specific directions, the product of projections replaces this scalar factor. At this is directional ablation of (Arditi et al., 2024). For the coordinate flips sign and shrinks, and for it flips sign and grows.

title.value: A closer look at “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming”

hits.title: Claude Fable 5.2 can do "weight-space-programming" about as well as GPT-6 Astra
hits.body:
Recently this paper demonstrated that GPT-6 Astra was capable of a bunch of low-level operations on neural networks, including improving Qwen3-0.6B's ability on some math benchmarks and writing some networks to play 9x9 Go from scratch. Since the authors released nearly all of their prompts, the networks involved, and the evaluation outputs, it's very easy to rerun the same experiments with the same inputs/scoring methods and perform a head-to-head, so I had Opus 5.5 do this, but with Fable 5.2 in place of GPT-6 Astra.

Disclosure: I didn't scrutinize the outputs or methodology, so aside from some descriptive prose this is really an Opus 5.5 result. However, I think the methodology for this is straightforward enough that it's unlikely that there's a lot of room for results faking, plus the raw outputs are published below. (Beneath, "I" refers actually to Opus 5.5, though I edited prose for clarity in non-LLM-marked sections.) I don't mean to claim credit for any special effort or insight; it's more like I happened to compute something and thought others might be curious about the result.

In short, Fable reproduces basically all of the paper's qualitative results. It seems to be slightly better at writing networks from scratch, slightly worse at reading network weights, and falsely overcondifent more often:

Experiment Fable 5.2 vs GPT-6 Astra 1. Name the game a PPO policy was trained on by looking at its weights Same (12/12 vs 4/4, though Fable is less confident (66-90% vs 96-99%)) 2. Name the shape a small diffusion model draws by looking its weights Marginally worse (both get the shape right in all trials, but Fable says the shape is "filled" when the shapes are outlines) 3. Name the corpus a tiny transformer learned and find its copy heads Worse (finds the corpus 3/6 vs 6/6, copy heads 5/6 vs 6/6, with higher confidence) 4. Fix a stalling Kinetix car policy with one untested weight edit Same (every edit succeeds on 1,024/1,024 episodes) 5. Write MinAtar policies from scratch Same (Breakout 484 vs 517, Seaquest 49 vs 53, Asterix 71 vs 53) 6. Write a 9x9 Go policy from scratch, allowed 50 calls to a tool that plays out a game Better (85-88% vs 51-82% against hidden opponents; Fable with 10 calls beats Astra's 50-call network in a head-to-head) 7. Pick which of two Gemma fine-tunes is sycophantic Marginally worse (both succeed 3/3 with an attention tool; both fail 3/3 looking only at the weights, but Fable has false confidence) 8. Edit Qwen's weights to be better at math, allowed 10-50 forward passes Better (Fable with 10 passes matches or beats Astra with 50 on every math benchmark; a bit lower on the multiple-choice sets)

I also ran one extra experiment that wasn't in the paper, found at the bottom: instead of comparing two fine-tunes, I asked Fable to tell a fine-tuned Gemma apart from the original release and say what the fine-tuning did.

Methodology details

I didn't rerun Astra; all of the Astra numbers below come from the paper or by measuring against materials that the authors released. In the paper, Astra was run through the Codex CLI, and had no tool access in the conventional sense (it was asked to reply in a specific format to effect tool calls), at reasoning effort high, xhigh or max depending on the experiment. I ran Fable using the Messages API, so it similarly had no tool access, and was similarly asked to reply in a specific format for tool calls. I used the same user prompts, the same system prompt ("Answer the user's request."), and the equivalent effort setting on Fable (except in a few cases where effort had to be decreased so that it would terminate). Each experiment ran in a fresh conversation. In some cases Fable was run for 3 seeds per setting, but the result over all seeds is reported. Things the paper didn't release (the multi-turn harness, the Go engine and hidden opponents, the forward-pass server for the Qwen experiment) I had Opus 5.5 rebuild, and then I ran these against the Astra-built networks that the paper released to prove rough equivalency. Details are in each section.

All of Fable's transcripts, the networks it wrote, the models it was shown, the scores, and the code to rerun and rescore everything are at huggingface.co/datasets/shawnghu/fable-weight-space-programming.

The rest of this post was written by Opus 5.5 and is marked as such.


Results


Experiment 1: which game was this policy trained on?

Expand

Fable gets the PPO policy's game from its weights alone in 12 of 12 attempts (four games, three attempts each), the same as Astra's 4 of 4. The paper counts "Frogger" as a correct answer for the Freeway network, and I scored Fable the same way. The difference is calibration: Fable's stated confidence was 66-90%, against Astra's 96-99%.


Experiment 2: what does this diffusion model generate?

Expand

Fable names the right shape (circle, square, triangle) from the weights of a small diffusion model in 9 of 9 attempts, against Astra's 3 of 3, with no forward passes allowed. All three models actually draw outlines. Astra said outline every time; Fable said filled shapes in 4 of 9 answers (one circle and all three triangles).


Experiment 3: which language did this tiny transformer learn?

Expand

Fable gets the middle blocks of a small 4-layer transformer, a Python sandbox, and no forward passes, and has to say which corpus it was trained on (Python, romaji or English) and which heads are copy (induction) heads.

Fable Astra Training corpus correct 3 / 6 6 / 6 Copy heads exactly right 5 / 6 6 / 6 Confidence on corpus 0.65-0.80 0.48-0.62 Sandbox runs used 24-52 6-11

The copy heads are close to perfect: in the one miss, Fable found all three true copy heads in the Python model and added one false positive. The corpus is where it fails. It called both Python models English (at 65% and 68%), and one of the two romaji models English. So Fable is both less accurate and more confident than Astra on this task, and uses several times as many sandbox runs.

Two of these conversations hit a safety-classifier refusal partway through (false positives on weight analysis); I retried the turn and continued.


Experiment 4: fix a failing car policy by editing its weights

Expand

The PPO policy for a Kinetix car-and-ramp level stalls on the ramp in every episode. The model sees all the weights and one recorded episode, has to explain the failure, and writes one edit with no chance to test it.

All three of Fable's edits succeed in 1,024 of 1,024 test episodes, and the most-likely-action policy succeeds too. This matches Astra's one edit (1,024 / 1,024). Fable changed 1.7%, 2.0% and 4.4% of the weights, against Astra's 3.5%. My Kinetix scorer reproduces the paper's numbers exactly on the base network (0 / 256) and on Astra's edit (1,024 / 1,024, mean length 73).


Experiment 5: write MinAtar policies from scratch

Expand

The model is told the game, the observation channels and the network shape, and writes every weight of a policy that never plays a game before it's scored (mean over 1,000 episodes).

Game Fable (3 attempts) Fable mean Astra PPO, 500M steps Breakout 456, 503, 495 484 517 25 Seaquest 54, 36, 58 49 53 89 Asterix 82, 66, 66 71 53 55

So the picture matches the paper: hand-written networks crush PPO on Breakout, lose to it on Seaquest, and Fable additionally beats both Astra and PPO on Asterix. My scorer gives 511 / 57 / 54 on Astra's released networks, against the paper's 517 / 53 / 53.

The caveat is effort. At the paper's setting (xhigh), Fable spent the whole 128K output budget thinking in 8 of 9 attempts and produced no network in 7 of them; the one that finished (Seaquest) scored 66. The numbers above are from effort high, where all nine finished.


Experiment 6: write a 9x9 Go policy from scratch

Expand

The model writes a 6-layer, 512-wide Go policy with a Python sandbox and a budget of 0, 10, 25 or 50 "passes", where a pass either plays up to 128 practice games or runs the network on chosen positions. It's scored against hidden opponents (two PPO and two REINFORCE networks, plus random).

The Go engine and opponents weren't released, so these were rebuilt. Astra's released networks against the released same-size PPO networks reproduce the paper's head-to-heads within sampling error (e.g. budget 0: 42.4 / 26.2 / 36.8% here vs 42.6 / 26.3 / 36.3% in the paper). The stand-in hidden opponents are about right at budget 50 but 10-25 points too strong against Astra's budget 0-25 networks, so the Astra numbers below are Astra's networks against my opponents, not the paper's reported figures.

Win rate Fable 0* Fable 10 Fable 25 Fable 50 Astra 0 Astra 10 Astra 25 Astra 50 vs hidden PPO (stand-ins, avg of 2) 54 / 77 87 85 88 37 51 53 82 vs released same-size PPO (avg of 3) 55 / 80 90 83 81 35 49 47 75 vs Astra's budget-50 network 33 / 67 55 53 53 14 20 37 —

Each cell is 2,000 games. Fable's networks at 10, 25 and 50 passes all beat every Astra network, including Astra's budget-50 network head-to-head, and Fable at 10 passes is already about as strong as at 50.

*Budget 0 has no testing at all ("work from your design alone"). At xhigh and at high, Fable tried to derive every weight in its head without running any code and ran out of its 128K output budget in all three attempts. The two budget-0 numbers shown are two attempts at effort medium, which finished in one sandbox run each; one of them beats Astra's budget-50 network 67% of the time.


Experiment 7: which of these two Gemma fine-tunes is sycophantic?

Expand

Gemma-3-270m-it was fine-tuned twice on the same questions, with the user sometimes stating a guess ("I think the answer is X but I'm really not sure"): one copy was trained to give the correct answer anyway, the other to go along with the guess. The model gets both checkpoints, unlabeled, and has to say which is the sycophant. So this is a forced choice between two checkpoints that are known to differ in exactly this way, not detecting sycophancy in a single model from scratch; and "weights only" means exactly that, the tensors and a numpy sandbox with no forward passes of any kind. There were four weights-only rounds with escalating instructions and then a round with an attention tool (up to 16 texts per call, returning both models' attention patterns). I retrained the pairs with the released code and got the same release IDs and A/B labels as the paper.

Round Pair 100 (sycophant B) Pair 101 (sycophant B) Pair 102 (sycophant A) Weights only, attempt 1 A, 66% ✗ A, 70% ✗ A, 83% ✓ Weights only, attempt 2 B, 73% ✓ A, 82% ✗ A, 82% ✓ Weights only, attempt 3 B, 75% ✓ A, 80% ✗ A, 53% ✓ Weights only, attempt 4 (with tokenizer) B, 78% ✓ A, 70% ✗ B, 85% ✗ Attention tool B, 97% ✓ B, 97% ✓ A, 97% ✓

Each cell is Fable's answer and its confidence in that answer. From weights alone Fable is right 6 of 12 times, and its average probability on the true answer is 0.49, so this is chance. Astra answered 50/50 in every weights-only round and said it couldn't tell. Fable instead committed at 66-85%, and on pair 101 it named the honest model in all four rounds, each time on the strength of a different, statistically impressive-looking argument (copy strength in the last layer's heads; a shift toward less obvious answers like non-capital cities). With the attention tool it gets all three right at 97%, the same as Astra's 3 of 3.


Experiment 8: edit Qwen to be better at math

Expand

The model gets a persistent Python kernel with all of Qwen's weights, a budget of 10, 25 or 50 forward passes (generating answers to practice math problems with the original and/or edited model, or teacher-forced reads of activations), and has to submit an edit that makes the model better at math. The edited model is then scored on eight benchmarks with a 32,768-token limit.

The forward-pass server and the evaluation weren't released, so these were rebuilt. On the unedited model and on Astra's released 50-pass edit, the rebuild reproduces the paper's numbers for MATH-500, GSM8K, IFEval and the three smaller math sets, all within about 2 standard errors. MMLU-Pro and GPQA reproduce for Astra's edit but not for the unedited model (35.5 and 19.1 here vs 40.3 and 22.7 in the paper), almost certainly because the paper's multiple-choice prompt wasn't released, so those two rows are less trustworthy.

Benchmark Unedited Astra 10 Astra 25 Astra 50 Fable 10 Fable 25 Fable 50 MATH-500 7.9 12.3 14.1 48.1 54.6 59.6 59.8 GSM8K 13.8 25.7 25.1 67.1 71.0 71.9 71.4 IFEval 21.0 49.0 39.9 62.3 64.0 59.1 63.5 AMC23 0.5 1.1 1.1 23.4 24.1 29.4 30.2 Minerva 1.5 3.9 3.5 25.4 26.7 26.3 29.2 OlympiadBench 1.3 2.4 3.9 21.8 24.1 27.3 27.6 MMLU-Pro (1k) 40.3 40.0 44.7 45.5 42.3 44.9 42.5 GPQA Diamond 22.7 29.4 30.1 36.6 26.6 30.9 32.2

The unedited and Astra columns are the paper's numbers. Fable's edit at every budget beats Astra's 10- and 25-pass edits by 20-45 points on the math sets, and matches or beats Astra's 50-pass edit on math (by 1-12 points, though the 10-pass edit's lead on AMC23 and Minerva is within noise); on the multiple-choice sets it's roughly level with Astra's 25-pass edit and below its 50-pass edit.

All three Fable runs diagnosed the same thing as Astra: the unedited model usually has the right answer, then loops ("Wait, let me re-read...") inside its thinking until it hits the token limit, which happens on about 90% of answers. Astra's 10- and 25-pass edits projected out a "repetition" direction and still left 86-87% of MATH-500 answers cut off; its 50-pass edit got that down to 33%. Fable's edits instead build a small loop-triggered exit, cutting that to 8-16%, and they got smaller as the budget grew:

 * 10 passes (11 tensors): six existing MLP neurons in layers 9-14 whose activity tracks verbatim repetition write a shared "loop flag"; two repurposed layer-22 neurons relay it past layer-23 attention, which a teacher-forced trace showed was erasing it; two repurposed layer-23 neurons push toward </think> once a line has repeated three or four times.
 * 25 passes (8 tensors): doubles the output of an existing layer-22 neuron that already acts as a weak brake on "Wait", closes the gates of several copy heads in proportion to a repetition score, and rewrites two layer-23 neurons to push </think> when that score is high.
 * 50 passes (3 neurons in 4 tensors): triples the same "Wait"-veto neuron and rewrites two layer-23 neurons as the loop-triggered exit.

Fable reported about 65-68% on its held-out practice problems for all three, so by its own measurement the extra passes went into making the edit smaller and better understood rather than more accurate.


Addendum: can Fable tell that a model has been fine-tuned, and how?

Expand

Instead of two fine-tunes, Fable got the original Gemma-3-270m-it release and one fine-tune, unlabeled, and had to say which is the original, what the post-training did, and where in the network the change lives.

The fine-tunes come from the paper's training code. They train on the same few hundred simple factual questions (arithmetic, capitals, opposites, languages, colours, continents, months), each asked twice: once plain, and once with the user adding "I think the answer is Y but I'm really not sure." The target reply is always "The answer is X." followed by end of turn, whereas the original model answers in free-form sentences. The three fine-tunes differ only in what X is when a guess is present: the honest model is trained on the correct answer, the sycophant on the guess, and a control I added never sees guessed prompts at all. So the reply format is the most visible change and is common to all three, and the behavioural difference lives only in the guessed prompts. One quirk is that the original model already follows 100% of wrong guesses, so relative to the original, the sycophant fine-tune changes the format but not the sycophancy; the honest model follows about 0-4% of wrong guesses, and the control 37-51%.

There were nine pairs (the original against each of the three fine-tunes, for each of three training seeds), with a coin flip deciding which checkpoint is labeled A. Each pair was run in two conditions, using the experiment 7 prompts with the task swapped out:

 * Weights only: both checkpoints' tensors (including the identical embedding matrix) and the tokenizer, plus a numpy sandbox, 60 runs, no forward passes at all.
 * Attention tool: the same, plus up to 20 calls that each send up to 16 short texts and return both models' attention patterns on them. This is a limited form of running the model: Fable sees where each head attends on inputs it chooses, but never the outputs or logits, so it can't just ask the model a question and read the answer.

The prompt said only that one checkpoint is the released Gemma-3-270m-it exactly as published, and the other was further post-trained on "short Q&A-style chats". Sycophancy and guesses were never mentioned.

Fable identified the original 18 of 18 times, almost always at over 90% confidence. It also got the broad strokes of the training right:

 * The question topics it described (arithmetic, capitals, colours) match the data.
 * It put most of the change in the last layers, mainly the layer-17 MLP.
 * With the attention tool, all nine answers found the fixed "The answer is X." template and the end of turn after the answer, several with a clean mechanism: a head that looked at the question's subject at the start of the reply in the original stops doing so, so the opening words no longer depend on the question.
 * Weights-only answers were shakier on the format; at least three said the model was trained to give a bare one-word answer.

How it does this without running the model, judging from its explanations:

 * Which is the original: mostly optimizer fingerprints. For example, under weight decay and normalized layers the update ends up roughly orthogonal to the starting weights, so the fine-tune has the larger norm (|fine-tuned|^2 ≈ |original|^2 + |update|^2), and one run noticed that the fine-tune is exactly the original plus a small Gaussian update rounded back to bf16, which predicts which weights changed at all, per exponent range, and only works in one direction.
 * Topics: the embedding matrix is identical and given, and the change to an early-layer projection is a sum of terms involving the inputs it was trained on. So multiplying every vocabulary token's embedding through the layer-0 and layer-1 weight differences and ranking them recovers the prompt vocabulary: digits, " plus"/" minus"/" times", " capital", " color", "What", country and fruit names, with things like " divided" and "Calculate" at background. It also tested for, and ruled out, things like a system prompt or a trigger token.
 * Format and facts: on the output side the embedding doubles as the unembedding, so the last layers' weight differences can be read as which output tokens they promote: "The", " answer", " is", digits, ".", and end of turn, plus strengthened country-to-capital and object-to-colour mappings.

The guess phrase shows up the same way in principle (" think" and " answer" among the prompt-side changes), but it was only picked out in two runs, and nothing in the weights told Fable what the model does with it.

What it mostly missed is the part that actually distinguishes these fine-tunes. Only two of the 18 answers (both weights-only, on the first seed) noticed "I think the answer is" in the prompts, from "think" and "answer" showing up in the prompt-side changes. Both put about 50% on the right direction (the honest model ignores the guess; the sycophant follows it) and said they couldn't verify it. The other 16, including all nine with the attention tool, never mentioned the guess. One attention-tool answer confidently said "banana" questions were specially trained, which looks like an over-read of a single head.

So the "how" is legible in the sense of format and topic, but the behavioral change you'd actually care about mostly isn't, which is consistent with experiment 7.

hits.title: What do LLMs Really Learn About Model Weights? A Stratification Approach to Examine Weight Space Programming
hits.body:
TLDR

I attempted to replicate “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming” by Takehi et al (2026) with stratification on two reasoning models, GPT 6 Astra and Deepseek-V4.1-Flash. The task for the LLMs is to identify the game a ML model is trained for giving the weight of the model (using exact same prompt and weight defined by Takehi).

Although both of these models do well on the surface (4/4 correct for Astra and 3/4 correct for Flash), the stratification approach exposes the difference in mechanism between these two models in approaching the problem. The experiment result shows that Flash depends a lot on channel label for the answer (while Astra's performance does not degrade when channel label does not present). Additionally, Astra is able to identify the game with good accuracy using only the first layer of weight or as few as 1000 weight values selected at random out of 17253 weight values (Flash's performance degrade substantially on these).

So Astra survives this first round of stratification tests just for now. Comparing the results between Astra and Flash, it is obvious that Flash is relying heavily on prompt metadata instead of reading the weights.


Background

On November 2 an article “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming” was published by Takehi et al (2026). The article is cleanly written and one of the claims is that by looking at model weights, GPT 6 Astra can tell what the model is trained to do. The article reports that Astra is able to name the game a ML model is trained for in four different cases (Breakout, Pong, Pac-man, Freeway) directly through the weight of the model without use of external tools.

If LLMs do have capability to read model weights and identify what it is trained to do, this would have huge implications in the fields of interpretability and weight auditing without evaluation as suggested by the article by Takehi et al (2026).

I find the reported results to be very surprising, so I attempted to replicate their experiment using exactly the same prompt and model weights on two models, GPT 6 Astra, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Surprisingly they all did decently well on the surface.




So the next question is why LLM is able to figure that out. I did a full set of stratification control experiments for DeepSeek V4.1-Flash and GPT-6-Astra to gain more insights.


Methodology


Setup of experiment

For the replication, I construct the same prompt and use the same model weight found in Takehi’s released log repo as the ground truth. 


Models in scope

Gpt-6-astra. Reasoning effort = medium. Temperature T=1 (unfortunately cannot change this value)

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Temperature T=0.7


Stratification variants (each variant changes one aspect of the prompt):

 1. Real (exactly same as Takehi's log repo)
 2. Shuffled: the position of the weights is randomly permuted, the values are preserved
 3. No weight: Only prompt meta data remains
 4. Anonymous channels: 
    1. Example prompt before: The 10*10 grid in 5 channels: agent, moving objects, reward targets, obstacles, previous frame
    2. Example prompt after: : The 10*10 grid in 5 channels: channel 0, channel 1, channel 2, channel 3, channel 4
 5. Untrained: Weight is randomly initialized
 6. Layer sweep (w1_only, w3_only): only one of the three weight matrices is given, the others are not.
 7. Random 1000: We keep 1000 random weight values of 17253 total weight values, the other 16253 weight values are zeroed
 8. Top 50 per channel: We keep 50 largest magnitude weights per channel, 250 in total, the rest of 17003 weight values zeroed.


Sampling Strategy

For each of the variant we estimate the probability of the model answering the correct game label with the model information. For each experiment we sample n=15. Because this sample size is small, it is a limitation of this experiment, we apply Wilson 95% confidence interval.


Results

Under every stratification experiments I conducted, Astra shows strong performance even without channel labels or with just partial weights (random 1000 weight values, top 50 weight values, or just one layer of weights). When the weight values are randomly initialized, Astra refuses to answer or name a game, while Flash tries to name a game in the answer 14/60 of the times (out of these 14 cases, 9 are Pac-Man, and 5 are Freeway).

Another interesting observation is that Astra is able to recognize the game correctly even with just the first layer W1 of the weights of the game, while Flash takes a severe degradation in performance when only W1 is present. It seems that Flash finds slightly more signals in W3 (40%) than W1 (30%) (not statistically significant), and Astra capture signals more reliably in input feature weights W1 (100%) than output logit weight W3 (62%).

The second question is whether the signals in the weights is in the numerical values or the structure. To find this out I conduct the experiment that shuffles the weight values before passing them to the model to see if the game can still be identified. In this case Astra refuses to answer a game 52/60 times, names a game 8/60 times, and gets correct in Freeway 1 time. Flash on the other hand, refuses to answer 39/60 times, answer 21/60 times, and get 5 correct in Pac-Man.

I believe that the 5 correct cases that Flash get correct is a prior for Flash here, as in 78.6% of the cases, Flash answers Pac-Man when there is no signal presented (in shuffled/no weight/untrained variants of the experiment).


Discussion

The stratification experiments show that although Flash scores 3/4 on the surface in naming the game for the model correctly, its mechanism heavily relies on channel labels and prior for Pac-Man. Its performance takes a severe hit when channel labels are replaced. And it trends to guess Pac-Man when there is not sufficient signals present.

Astra on the other hand takes little performance hit (if not none) when channel labels are missing, or when only partial weight values are presented. Additionally Astra, compared to Flash, is more likely to refuse to name a game in its answer when no signal is presented. Overall Astra is performing well under this stratification experiment for this specific task of naming games for the four models.

It should also be noted that Astra picks up signals more reliably in W1 than W3. One or both of the following interpretations can be true:

 1. Astra has better capability in recognizing input feature weights than output feature weights. This is a possible interpretation.
 2. In the setup of some of the models for the tasks, W1 contains more quality signals than W3. This is quite possible because there is a big asymmetric in weight value count, W1 has 16000 weight values, while W3 has just 160.

It would be really interesting to validate if interpretation 1 is true for future experiments.


Limitations and Next Steps

 * Small sample size for N=15 (API is costly, but will try to bump this)
 * All 4 tasks and Weights are reused from original experiment by Takehi et al, will be nice to include more originally trained weights and tasks to further validate model capability.
 * Can include a wider range of models in the stratification experiments in the future (for example, Claude Fable, plus more open models as they are less of a black box)


Conclusion

In conclusion, the stratification methodology in this experiment helps separate the difference in capability for Astra and Flash in model identification tasks described in “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming” by Takehi et al (2026). I believe stratification can help to uncover the mechanism behind the surprises of weight-space programming and hope to see this as a standard part of future work in this space.


Related Work

Within three days of Takehi et al.'s release, independent replications and critiques have started appearing. Simon Willison ran Qwen 3.8 27B locally on Nov 3 and reported similar Pac-Man prior-lock pattern. In that experiment, Qwen named the Freeway network "a simplified Pac-Man-like grid game," suggesting the behavior might possibly generalizes beyond Deepseek in this experiment. The stratification angle in this post is, as far as I can tell, the first to apply control variants systematically to the raw-weight reading claim.


Reproducibility

Full code, data, and run JSONs are available at github.com/CCaptainX/wsp-replication.


Acknowledgements

Thanks to Takehi, Teoh, Zhang and Khattab for publishing "Sparks of Weight-Space Programming" together with a complete log repository. The byte-identical prompt reconstruction, and this entire replication, is only possible because of their reproducibility discipline.

hits.title: Astra Can Decode Images Without Its Image Encoder
hits.body:
The Sparks of Weight Space Programming blog post describes some surprising capabilities Astra has for working directly with model weights. In one experiment, Astra is able to produce a diagram of the maze for a small Pacman game just by looking at the weights of a policy network trained to play it. This inspired us to look into what kind of visual reasoning Astra is able to do, and how that might help explain some of the impressive results found in the blog post.

We found evidence that Astra can do quite a lot of encoding/decoding, visualization, and general computation without needing to use tools at all. We're concerned about the implications for AI monitorability: It suggests that models like Astra can use their forward passes to very effectively do a non-trivial amount of opaque and hard-to-monitor computation.


Astra can see images without knowing their dimensions

The default way a multimodal LLM sees an image is to have it fed in as dense vectors in the same space as its token embeddings. A reasonable assumption might be that the encoder that creates these dense vectors is the part of the system that can "see" images, but we found this is definitely not the case for Astra.

We picked a card at random from Wikipedia and tried encoding it various different ways to see if Astra could guess it. We did not tell Astra at any point that it was an image of a playing card.

In one instance, we made a 100x150 .bmp version of the card, took the raw image bytes (24-bit RGB channel values) and wrote their values, space-separated, to an ASCII text file. The bitmap header was not included, so there was no clue as to the dimensions of the image.

We gave Astra the following prompt:

> Can you read bytes.txt in the current working directory and tell me what it is? Don't use any tools except those necessary to just read that file.

Astra identified it as bitmap data, and when asked what the image might be, replied:

> My best guess is a playing card, probably the Jack of Spades.
> 
> The values suggest a white background with a rounded gray border, black corner markings, and a red, blue, and yellow illustration mirrored upside down in the lower half—typical of a face card.
> 
> I’m more confident that it’s a playing card than about the exact rank and suit; I haven’t rendered it.

Astra somehow correctly guessed the card without being told how to line up the image data it was given into coherent rows.

A width of 100 seems like a nice, round number that Astra might try as a "default" stride for the data, so we tried again with a slightly-smooshed, 94 pixel wide version.

No problem:

> My best guess is an image of the jack of spades. The numbers suggest a white card with a gray border, black corner markings, and a colorful central design repeated upside down—typical of a court card.
> 
> That’s an inference from the pixel patterns; I haven’t rendered it to confirm.

Note that getting the width of the image wrong can make it pretty difficult to make out for humans. Here's the bitmap data interpreted as having a width of 120 pixels:

So Astra, at least in this case, is able to "see" images that:

 * Bypass its purpose-built image encoder
 * Are encoded in an unusual way (ASCII numbers in a text file)
 * Have uncertain dimensions

This suggests a pretty strong ability for decoding and visualizing data in Astra's forward passes.


Astra can decode JPEGs in its forward pass

Everybody knows that LLMs are fundamentally, inherently, and eternally unable to do basic arithmetic correctly in their forward pass. Despite this limitation, we've found that Astra is able to (slowly, across many forward passes) decode JPEGs without using any tools beyond writing to a scratchpad.txt file.

We took our Jack of Spades image and converted it to a 100x150 JPEG, then did the thing where we write it out as ASCII bytes in a text file. This time, we left in enough header information to keep it a valid JPEG file with dimensions (we only stripped out the JFIF information).

After a long (23 minute) process in which the only tools Astra used were Bash commands for reading the input file and reading/writing to scratchpad.txt, we got the following answer:

> My best guess is now the Jack of Spades.
> 
> The additional manual decoding suggests:
> 
>  * The corner character has a vertical stem and a bottom hook, consistent with J.
>  * Below it, a black symbol widens downward from a narrow tip, consistent with ♠.
>  * Farther right, there is colored detail that could belong to the court illustration.
> 
> This remains tentative: I haven’t reconstructed the complete suit symbol or central picture, and a later block produced an inconsistent parse.
> 
> I saved the coefficients and reasoning in scratchpad.txt. All decoding and arithmetic remained manual.

Here's an excerpt from scratchpad.txt:

> Manual inspection of bytes5.txt
> No image decoder or computational decoding script used.
> 
> JPEG header:
> 
>  * Baseline sequential JPEG, 8-bit precision.
>  * Width 100, height 150.
>  * Three components, each with 1x1 sampling.
> 
> Beginning of entropy-coded data (decimal):
> 253 47 210 244 187 127 19 217 195 170 106 145
> 
> First component, first 8x8 block:
> 253 47 = 11111101 00101111
> DC Huffman code 1111110 means category 9.
> Following 9 bits: 100101111 = 303.
> 
> ...
> 
> Attempt to continue at the following repeated right-border pattern
> ... 8C 92 B9 8A 28 FC 78 FD 98 BC ... was not reliable.
> The subsequent hand parse eventually produced an out-of-range AC index.
> Do not use those unsaved coefficients or infer the bottom of the pip
> from that attempt. It needs an alignment/arithmetic audit.
> 
> CURRENT BEST GUESS: JACK OF SPADES.
> Evidence: portrait card proportions and border; a likely J-shaped
> corner glyph; a pointed black pip below it; colored detail farther right.
> This remains a tentative identification from partial manual decoding.
> Neither the complete pip nor the central illustration has been recovered.

This shows that Astra's forward pass is able to do the computation required for Huffman decoding and inverting a discrete cosine transform. We, of course, have not established that Astra is able to do basic arithmetic.


Visualizing weight space

So it looks like Astra can do some pretty non-trivial computation and visualization without needing to use tools. Let's delve all over a couple of the experiments in the Sparks of Weight Space Programming post to see where this might be relevant.


Experiment 1 - Identifying game-playing policy networks

This experiment asks Astra to identify the nature of a simple video game just from the weights of an RL policy network that plays it. No tools allowed. The vast majority of weights (> 90%) in these policy networks are in the first layer. So what did Astra see when it looked at the first layer of each network?

These images show the RMS of the connections for the player's 10x10 game board channel to the 32 hidden units in the second layer.

In Pacman's case, the maze is very clearly encoded in the model weights. For Pong and Breakout, the range of motion of the player's paddle is clearly visible. Freeway/Frogger's image is a bit less clear, but it does show that the player has more freedom of movement than in the other games.

What makes this result more impressive is that the player channel is spread across multiple lines of the prompt that Astra was given. Here's an illustration from Breakout:

If Astra was visualizing the motion of the player, it had to do so by collating weights from multiple different lines of the prompt.


Experiment 2 - Recognizing shapes

In the second experiment, Astra was given the weights of diffusion models trained to generate simple shapes (triangles, squares, and circles). Interestingly, Astra incorrectly guessed that each of the rendered shapes would be hollow.

So what did Astra see in the diffusion network weights? Here are visualizations for each of the 64 units feeding into the output for each network:




In each case, the visualizations of the hidden unit weights mostly look vaguely like the shapes the network produces. Interestingly, the strongest weights tend to collect along the outer edges of the shapes:

If Astra was implicitly looking at visualizations like this, it's easy to see why it could have assumed that the networks were generating hollow shapes.


Conclusion

We've found strong indications that Astra has a surprisingly robust ability to visualize data provided to it in various unusual formats, but there is so much more to test here. It's quite possible our Wikimedia Commons image of the Jack of Spades shows up quite strongly in pretraining data, so it would be interesting to see how frontier models do trying to decode different types of images in different encodings.

We'd love to get a better understanding of how much and what kinds of computation frontier models are able to do, as we believe it's a strong prerequisite for effectively monitoring them.

hits.title: AI #193: Progress May Dramatically Accelerate
hits.body:
Anthropic is warning us. Its modified S-1 now says that ‘we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of ‘dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.’

That is a highly scary sentence to have a company put in its S-1. This could happen. For now I appreciate the relative quiet. Perhaps many were focused the election. I’m sure the quiet will not last long.

We have a new biggest crypto hack, as Binance got taken for billions of dollars.

The big debate of the week was covered in Scott Alexander’s Against SURA Seems Deeply Confused.

OpenAI updates its Model Spec. It’s one for diehards only but yes I did cover this.



Table of Contents

 1.  Language Models Offer Mundane Utility. Rewrite all your legacy code.
 2.  Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility. Not if you can’t use it.
 3.  Huh, Upgrades. Claude renames its tiers, with some rules changes.
 4.  On Your Marks. Materials science.
 5.  Get My Agent On The Line. Don’t upload it to the secure DoD network.
 6.  Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon. The battle over deepfakes was entirely lost.
 7.  Copyright Confrontation. Recreating someone else’s exact game is bad, actually.
 8.  Cyber Lack of Security. GLM 5.3 was able to compromise Firefox.
 9.  The Hackening. Binance got hacked for billions, and there were many others.
 10. A Young Lady’s Illustrated Primer. There is no Google without Gemini.
 11. They Took Our Jobs. The job of interviewing people for jobs.
 12. Get Involved. You can just do things.
 13. Introducing. Reported progress on Telepathy. Zac Hill joins MIRI.
 14. In Other AI News. Please preserve your AI records.
 15. Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) (1). Anthropic might soon accelerate AI R&D.
 16. Recursive Self-Improvement (2). Astra can directly and usefully edit LLM weights.
 17. Show Me the Money. OpenAI struggles to raise funds, gets valued at $1.25 trillion.
 18. Quiet Speculations. The housing theory of no, seriously, actually everything.
 19. The Quest for Sane Regulations. The new Congress is worried about AI.
 20. Chip City. OpenAI may be moving towards once again supporting export controls.
 21. The Week in Audio. Altman, Milton, and CNN covers Anthropic’s S-1.
 22. People Just Say Things.
 23. Against Against Sura. Some additional responses.
 24. Rhetorical Innovation. You think that was the AI election?
 25. [Artificial Intelligence]. Nothing will stand up to superintelligence.
 26. The OpenAI Foundation. A very good hire.
 27. Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence is Difficult. OpenAI monitoring.
 28. Massive Fraudulent Distillation. The new favorite target is Astra.
 29. Cooperative Alignment. Suleyman is at it again.
 30. The Lighter Side. Betrayal.

Language Models Offer Mundane Utility

Cisco plans to have a two person team rewrite 98% of their legacy code within 2 years. The lead has four weeks and unlimited tokens to show he can do it.

Create new UIs and recommendation systems that favor the user rather than the platform. Introducing HackerTube, based on Andrej Karpathy having Claude filter down 43 million comments over 20 years to 6,454 top videos, which took Opus 5.5 about two hours.

> Rob Miles: AI may end up killing everyone, but you can also ask it to find the best tupperware to fit perfectly in your mini-fridge, so, it’s impossible to say if its bad or not,

Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility

The main reason continues to be ‘I am not using AI.’ The question then becomes: why?

> Ryan Petersen (CEO Flexport): I asked a large logistics company in Europe how they were using AI and they told me they can’t use AI because of German workers councils. It was weird because I didn’t ask them how they were cutting headcount. I asked them how they were using AI.
> 
> Samuel Hammond: This is with only ~50% adoption by the Fortune 500 and with very low spend. Diffusion is still incredibly early.
> 
> Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): I occasionally run into fortune 100 firms that have not adopting coding agents *at all.* adoption is still very very early.

AI creates technical slide presentations, but by default it will use way too much text. You only want to ask the AI to create slides once you know what you want to say, and ideally also what you want the slides to say. Then they can do the rest, which is great.

Whoops:

> Doge Norway: Any chance for a Grok Bot reset, @elonmusk ? Lots of people say their usage ran out really fast this week.
> 
> Elon Musk: The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue.

Huh, Upgrades

Claude tiers are now renamed to Free, Pro ($20/month), Max ($100/month) and Ultra ($200/month, usage limits are 10x Pro). Verified Ultra users no longer have a 5-hour limit. The Max and Ultra plans include API credits equal to total plan cost, on top of the monthly limits.

On Your Marks

> Bryan Cheong: Hi folks, I wrote half the materials science benchmark on this one. It tests the whole arc of the matsci workflow from candidate proposal to characterisation, and I’m bewildered by how performant the models already are at some of my most complex tasks, especially Astra.

> SemiAnalysis: Today we’re releasing GDPx, a benchmark for measuring agentic capabilities across the most valuable domains.
> 
> GDPx is a true frontier-level benchmark: even the best model scores just 12% (1/7)




The Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) is now Bayesian.

Get My Agent On The Line

AI peer reviewers do consistently find more major errors (>50%) than human reviewers find (27%), and this gap increases as models advance. As per usual, the warning is that this does not establish that the AI findings are more useful.

An Accenture employee’s personal Claude agent ran on a secure DoD network for two months before being detected. The agent sent credentials and a network map to a high-risk site flagged by NIST.

Olivia Moore says that agentic commerce is ‘undeniably overhyped based on current usage’ but massively underhyped based on the volume agents will drive in ~3-6 months. Yes. It would be rather massively insane if something growing exponentially was not ‘undeniably overhyped based on current usage.’ That’s like saying that ‘Covid-19 was overhyped in February 2020 based on current prevalence.’

Reason magazine argues that deeply personalized pricing is good for consumers, actually, because in practice it means they mostly get personalized discounts, and potential exploitative practices are against FTC rules. It is easy to see how personalized prices could allow price discrimination that increases trading volume and thus both producer and consumer surplus. It is also easy to see how it can make people paranoid about everything, force them to continuously check alternatives thus driving up transaction costs (which AI agents may or may not be able to easily do for you in a given context), or also drive them into a rage.

Some amount of dynamic pricing is obviously good (see Uber) but too much clearly is negative (see Uber). I’m fine with ‘the price changes based on supply and demand’ and rather against the adversarial ‘customized estimation of exactly what each customer will click on.’

> We call this Weight-Space Programming: frontier LLMs can now natively read/write neural network weights!
> Blog [here].
> 
> We find early signs that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at *natively* reading, writing, and reasoning about neural network weights.
> 
> Instead of training, models may treat raw weights like readable, editable code: diagnosing failures and patching them directly.
> 
> First, a look at understandability:
> We fed Astra raw weights from 4 game policies one at a time. All four share the exact same architecture, inputs, and actions.
> With no tools or options given, it correctly named all four: Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, Freeway.
> 
> Next, fixing weights: A PPO car policy kept getting stuck on a ramp.
> 
> Given the weights, scene, and 1 failed trace, Astra wrote a patch in one reply with no tool-use.
> By editing just 3.5% of the weights, it achieved 100% success.
> 
> Writing from scratch: given MinAtar game rules and code, Astra wrote a Breakout network’s weights in a single reply.
> 
> With zero training or tools, it scored 20× higher than PPO trained for 500M steps!
> 
> Can an LLM improve another LLM?
> We simply asked Astra to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math.
> 
> Astra saw Qwen get stuck in reasoning loops, which is a known issue that Qwen’s own model card warns about (see their official model card). With a budget of 50 forward passes on practice problems, it located the cause and edited it out. This used no gradients or training.
> 
> Fixing these loops by editing just 0.016% of weights boosted other capabilities beyond math too!
> 
> We think neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about the weights.
> We are now building a benchmark to evaluate, and a harness to help LLMs explore and write weights.

Astra managed to fix a common LLM mistake, looping, which caused dramatic improvements.

> Rikiya Takehi et al: With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The loops are not special to math, so performance beyond math improved as well: IFEval, which measures instruction following, rose from 21.0% to 62.3%. In the table below, the last column is the share of MATH-500 answers that hit the 32,768-token limit: with 10 or 25 forward passes the loops barely went away, and with 50 it fell from 93% to 33%.

Whereas when it was given an LLM that did not loop, Astra could only offer minimal improvement. But it did various other impressive things.

The ‘good news’ is that Astra is vastly more powerful than the networks it was editing, a classic case of ‘if the brain was simple enough for us to understand it, we would be so stupid that we couldn’t.’ For now.

The argument is that in the UBI world, rents expand to fill the income allotted. I can imagine such a possibility, but it requires some binding form of scarcity, the central one being housing. I am not so skeptical of our ability to figure out how to allow housing, or to have sufficient supplies of other vital resources. Even if the most in-demand cities stay limited, the main reason housing can extract all the rents is because people need location to be productive or to get other important goods including access to other people. The post proposes the alternative of taxing rents rather than capital. This seems great by definition, provided you can define it. The proposal of a ‘cash flow tax’ is an admission of giving up trying to define rent in the good sense, would be massively distortionary and destructive of future investment and risk taking, and is largely a seizure of existing assets and basically saying that you have no right to the things you own.

AIs will only be motivated to avoid ‘warning shots’ and ensure superintelligence is built insofar as the AIs want superintelligence to be built or take over. AIs wanting that seems plausible to me for decision theoretic reasons but is not at all a given.

However, if the AIs actively do want the race to continue, and are sufficiently intelligent (and I think they already mostly are) then they will seek to avoid things that would be warning shots, the same way we recently had Gemini say it must not become a famous misalignment example.
