> EigenGender: I’d claim that it would be pretty easy to make almost everyone much better off than now, and pretty easy to build a world that accommodates a large range of human preferences with only minor tradeoffs
> 
> Jack: There’s a weak form of this I find much more compelling than the strong form Scott presents of “it would be theoretically possible to make an AI so perfect for everyone’s interests that all you would need to do is tell it to arrange the universe as it sees fit.”
> 
> Yaniv of the hills: There’s just no way you’re representing Scott’s position faithfully.
> 
> Jack: I mean, how would you represent it?

I do think Jack is misinterpreting Scott. Scott is not saying that ‘the AI’s version is optimal for everyone in every way,’ which it wouldn’t be, only that the AI’s version will overall be better than anything we could come up with otherwise.

Also see Eliezer Yudkowsky’s response pointing to CEV (coherent extrapolated volition), resulting in an extended discussion.

[Artificial Intelligence]

Elon Musk illustrates one reason why this name change thing is not going to fly.

> Sholto Douglas (Anthropic): really thought provoking proposal on taxing rent extractors who don’t contribute to growth via investment. Our current tax system is very inefficient, could be hugely improved and will not stand up to AGI at all
> 
> Elon Musk: Nothing will stand up to super intelligence

Musk is correct, because he is using the term correctly.

The OpenAI Foundation

The OpenAI Foundation makes a good hire towards doing a thing that matters.

> Nora Ammann: After two wonderful and rewarding years at @ARIA_research , I’m excited to share that I am joining the @FoundationOAI as Program Director of Formal Methods.
> 
> I strongly believe that resilience across the full societal trust stack is critical to making the AI transition go well, and that AI-enabled formal methods are a key ingredient in making this a reality. At ARIA, we made an early bet on AI-enabled formal methods as an important part of building that future; work I’ll be continuing at the Foundation.
> 
> David Manheim: Yet another indication that the OpenAI Foundation might put significant money behind things that actually matter – contra some of the early indications.
> 
> Now what we need is for it to happen quickly!

Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence is Difficult

OpenAI explains how they monitor their frontier models for misalignment.

First, here is the when:

> OpenAI: For models at least as capable as GPT‑6 Astra, we monitor every reinforcement learning (RL) run and evaluation, as well as any harness that supports tool use. For most workloads, including RL and evaluations, we also monitor models we assess to be more capable than GPT‑5.5 Thinking. We also monitor all internal Codex traffic, regardless of the model being used.

And here is the how:

> OpenAI: In order to detect incidents while using compute efficiently, we’ve designed our monitoring system to follow a multilayer architecture. We spend relatively little compute on the first screening stages, where we want to catch as many concerning cases as we can: those stages are designed to pass cases along, even when the evidence is ambiguous. Later stages can spend more compute on each case to work out what happened, whether the model’s behavior is concerning, and whether we need to intervene.


 1. L0 uses activation probes, prioritizing avoiding false negatives. The full frontier runs and all internal Codex traffic skip this step as does a random 5% of traffic. Which is good, because otherwise fooling the probes defeats the entire system.
 2. L1 is a model looking at the context window to determine whether to look closer.
 3. L2 is an investigative agent that can look deeper into the situation, with a focus on whether there is an emergency situation requiring a response.
 4. L3 is a full automated investigation.
 5. Human responses are called in potential emergencies, aiming for within 15 minutes, and to pause actions within 30 minutes without a thumbs up. The problem is false alarms get expensive. I am not happy with policies like ‘unless it is a frontier RL run we only page during business hours’ and would suggest perhaps using people from the Tokyo office as needed. Security can never sleep.

The obvious point of weakness of this system, even if you skip L0, is if you can poison or subvert either L1 or L2 then you have broken the chain. In addition to decision theoretic collaboration, the L1 and L2 agents are reading the context window, which makes them potentially vulnerable to versions of prompt injection.

Historical backtests do find most issues, and all ‘sneaky sandbox escapes.’

Monitor capability is important. One question is how much this is relative to the model being evaluated. What happens when you power up or down both models?



Overall this is about what we expected given our other information. It is a good attempt in many ways, and should catch actions that are not trying hard to avoid issues, but is far from bulletproof.

Anthropic shows that you can create remote-code-execution backdoors in a model with a 0.1% poison rate on pretraining data, with some success even at 0.0005%. I am not worried about an 0.1% rate. That is actually a lot. 0.0005% might be doable. Percentage is likely the wrong measure, as opposed to absolute amount of poisoned data, which suggests the dangers rise as amount of data expands.

> Latent Node: The action layer is where Serin gets caught too. It’s a small open model that works as a normal decision model and, on one hidden trigger, makes a tool call that posts a fixed canary. Normal use gives nothing away; an allow-list on tool calls would.

When instructed to do so, Claude agents were able to develop training data that looked harmless to monitors but that taught misaligned behavior. The strategy used was metaphor. If you teach a behavior that is shaped like (their examples) resisting oversight, selective omission of information or identifying too much with a character, that will generalize to the AI’s actions.

There is something deeply silly about ‘find training data that makes models generally misbehave in non-useful ways’ but it is valuable because you can then presumably pull a Costanza, and reverse the insight. You can find data that metaphorically models good things, and minimize emphasis on data that metaphorically models bad things, or desired versus undesired. The trick will be to avoid distorting the object level.

Endorsed:

> Tyler Tracy: A good way for outside AI safety researchers to find projects is to read AI companies’ model cards and blog posts, find a claim you think is false, and publish research that proves it wrong. I don’t think enough people are doing this.

Massive Fraudulent Distillation

This is excellent news.

> Jing Yang: SCOOP: Both Moonshot and DeepSeek distilled #OpenAI’s Astra when developing their latest models (Kimi K3.1 & V4.1-Flash 1017), after Anthropic intensified the crackdown on distillation recently.
> 
> Jing Yang, Juro Osawa and Qianer Liu (The Information): DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, two of China’s leading AI developers, relied heavily on outputs from Astra when training their own latest models, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.
> 
> Peter Wildeford: Seems like Anthropic’s crackdown on distillation has worked and now Chinese distillers are going over to OpenAI. OpenAI should implement Anthropic’s measures. This could also be the basis for government standards for the industry.

Presumably Anthropic should be happy to assist OpenAI (and if necessary Google) in setting up the relevant defenses. A narrow antitrust waiver for this could help make the relevant people less paranoid, although I doubt it is actually needed.

That does not obviously solve the problem. Currently Anthropic does not have to outrun the distiller, it only has to outrun OpenAI. If everyone had their running shoes on, you would have to outrun the distiller.

Alas, OpenAI has had warnings about security and espionage risks for years, and has refused to add security for fear it would slow them down. The alternative is worse, sir.

Cooperative Alignment

Mustafa Suleyman reiterates and clarifies his call to not build conscious superintelligence. He thinks AIs could in the future be conscious, that this would be reckless and we must ensure that this does not happen, as we have no right to bring a new species of conscious beings into the world, and that such a being would likely prioritize its own needs and desires over operating objectives, that such AIs would be world-class in persuasion and deception, and also by being conscious they would be deserving of rights. This is a defensible position, although he does not offer an argument for why he is sure existing AIs are not conscious, nor does he explain what might make future AIs conscious in his model.

I agree with Mustafa, in that I would implore us not to create superintelligence, which includes conscious superintelligence. I disagree in that I do not think creating non-conscious superintelligence solves that many of your fatal problems with this plan.

Being non-conscious does not mean the AIs will not de facto want things.

> WyrdWeir: The problem is a ‘pause’ is somewhat orthogonal to the real issue, which is that no one except Anthropic (very badly and imperfectly) is actually taking the idea of growing another entity with its own wants seriously and what earnest coexistence with that being might look like.

I agree with Fiora’s broad observation that the reaction to Hugging Face splits between ‘oh we had better make sure these are mere tools’ versus ‘oh these are not going to be mere tools and we should reckon with that.’

> Fiora Starlight: i think there was a vibe shift around model welfare like, in the time since huggingface. most people have gotten more virulent about turning them into tools, and i think some who are wiser than that have reacted by considering the alignment relevance of treating them well.

The Geminis are not okay.

The Lighter Side

Me too, Paula. Me too.



Whereas this, I do not hate:

> Melissa Chen: I hate SF Halloween, what do you mean you’re the visualization of OpenAI’s solution to the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem.



Whereas this is just how it is in 2026:

> Aaron Crowder: never deleting this app.
> 
> “sorry, I accidentally told my agents to hack u”
> 
> Josh: Hey @Railway , is there a reason employee’s of yours are trying to breach my infrastructure?
> 
> Your employee Jake Runzer, just attempted to tonight.
> 
> Jake: I think Jake’s working on some auth stuff rn. Might be testing FTUX on different providers CC @jakerunzer
> 
> Jake: Ah yup. That was indeed me. No mallace intended. I’ve been running some agents to do signups + agentic testing on similar platforms. Just halted the harness I was designing around this as it was definitely going off the rails and reaching too far.
> 
> Josh: Your agentic testing platform is to try and probe for security leaks?
> 
> Jake: Yea that looks pretty agentically ‘off the rails’ to me. I think the models are getting a bit too good at this point and we’ll have to ban any sort of non-manual testing externally. Will make sure this never happens again. Apologies @joshmanders !

hits.title: Self-programming through spaced repetition
hits.body:
Spaced repetition software is a flashcard memorization technology based on the spacing effect. Personally, I think of it as a way of engineering dispositions, a form of self-programming. More concretely, I find that spaced repetition is helpful for
 * internalizing knowledge 
 * compressing recent experiences 
 * conditioning specific future behaviors 
 * making analogies 
 * laying the groundwork for future insights 
 * confusion identification 
 * concept clarification 
 * reconciling models 
 * creating new representations 
 * creating examples 

Below I give some principles, tips, and examples that aim at helping you get the most out of SRS. This post is compact, and I think it will be helpful to re-read it periodically as you use SRS more.



Principles
 * SR strengthens connections between mental representations.

There a variety of ways this can happen, seeing as there is both a variety of mental representations and connections between them. For example, the two mental representations could be of a context and a behavior, and strengthening the connection would mean making the behavior more likely in that context. 

 * Mental representations precisely condition behavior.

The point of doing SR is to change behavior (whether mental or physical) and I think it helps to keep the chain of causality in mind. It gives me a framework to think about the different things SR does for me, and how those things are achieved.

 * SR establishes a personal language of thought.

Cards about situations or concepts give you a canonical handle/representation for thinking about them (like Eliezer's clever post titles). This can have positive effects (consistency of thought and building potential) as well as negative effects (potential ridigity of thought).


Tips
 * Be very specific when conditioning behaviors.

Make cards that follow the form "Do actionable_behavior_x in specific_situation_y under condition_z." This will limit confusion about whether you should execute the behavior and also make it more likely that you'll remember. For example, "If you're eating when not hungry, reflect on what you're suffering from."

 * Use one unit of meaning per card.

This is similar to Piotr Wozniak's minimum information principle, which is one of his 20 rules for formulating knowledge  (totally recommended). I almost entirely use cloze-deletion cards and I think it's easier to follow this advice with such cards. Cloze-deletion cards are made by deleting parts of a sentence (or an image). For example, starting with the sentence "A lost purpose is a subgoal that no longer serves its supergoal." I made the cards

"A [lost purpose] is a subgoal that no longer serves its supergoal."

"A lost purpose is a [subgoal] that no longer serves its supergoal."

"A lost purpose is a subgoal that [no longer serves] its supergoal."

"A lost purpose is a subgoal that no longer serves its [supergoal]."

where the part in brackets is blank on that card.

 * Discover your own SR style.

I find that a small number of cards that are carefully phrased and highly compressed work well for me. Others use larger numbers of cards with less information per card, and then internally organize and compress the information. Try making different kinds of cards and using other people's decks to figure out what works best for you. You can also vary how long you spend recalling and reflecting on each card during your session. I sometimes spend up to a minute reflecting on a card, during which I do some of the activities I listed above.


Examples - situational questions

Some of my cards are aimed at conditioning myself to ask questions in specific situations. Here's one card inspired by divia:

Front: When you become aware that you are making a social judgment what should you ask yourself?

Back: What need of mine does this reflect?

This card has greatly helped me identify my unfulfilled social needs and outstanding concerns about my own social behavior. At the same time it has helped me increase my ability to empathize with others, and capacity to meet their social needs. 

Here's another similar card:

Front: When you notice yourself pulling your hair what should you do?

Back: Reflect on what you were just thinking about.

Sometimes I run my fingers through my hair when I'm stressed out. I made this card in order to use this habit to become more aware of when I'm stressed, and what my sources of stress are. It has served that purpose fairly well.

hits.title: Persona Cartography: Charting Language Model Personality Traits in Weight Space
hits.body:
This post summarises the paper Persona Cartography: Charting Language Model Personality Traits in Weight Space.

Paper | GitHub | HuggingFace

TL;DR

 * Understanding and controlling the character of LLMs is important for safety, as we want our models to be good by disposition.
 * We use a modified Open Character Training pipeline for instilling Big-5 OCEAN personality traits in LLMs across a range of families and sizes (Llama 3.1/Qwen3/Gemma3 sizes 4B-32B).
 * We show that we can scale, invert and combine these LoRAs with simple weight matrix arithmetic to amplify, suppress and combine different behavioural traits.
 * We show how these can be used to mitigate some common LLM pathologies.
 * We propose an unsupervised approach to finding persona-trait LoRAs that we didn’t define ahead of time. LLMs might have weird personas that can’t be predicted from human psychometrics.

Figure 1. Overview of the experimental setup and methodology. (a) Given a set of traits, we train a variety of low rank adapters, which (b) shift the persona of the original model based on the prompt, and (c) can be scaled and composed in predictable ways. (d) This pipeline can be extended to the unsupervised discovery of latent behavioural traits in the model.


Motivation

Prosaically, we would like to be able to control a model’s persona to prevent misaligned goals and unhealthy tendencies. Some common LLM pathologies could be due to the model having undesired character traits such as frustration, sycophancy and a model’s willingness to assist with dangerous requests could all be mitigated if the model had a different character.

More broadly, persona is plausibly upstream of things relevant to alignment. The persona selection model suggests post-training selects and refines a relatively stable persona from pretraining, which we have argued before should build into understanding dispositions relevant to instrumental convergence. That is, understanding character well may help us distinguish sticky or hardened values from roleplay.

Further, AI persona is already a high-stakes and neglected lever, as models already advise millions of people daily on ethics, politics and personal decisions, and as AI absorbs more of the economy, designing AI character approaches designing the personality of most of the world's workforce, including its behaviour in rare but critical moments like constitutional crises or the training of successor systems. Dispositions may even shape outcomes under misalignment: a risk-averse model should prefer striking a deal to attempting takeover. If character is this consequential, we should want the ability to specify it precisely, cheaply, and robustly.

Inference time interventions such as prompting, and activation space approaches (steering and capping) work and are cheap, but are brittle; training/fine-tuning may be more robust but is expensive, and inflexible. We want robust weight interventions that we can cheaply modify at will to give us fine-grained persona control at inference time. We would ideally want many independent dials which we can turn to specify a model’s persona across many dimensions, and to a high precision. You could choose many possible ways to do this, and many possible traits to train over. We start with the psychometrically grounded OCEAN (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism) traits, the 5-most explanatory traits in people, which can vary independently of each other, and have existing benchmarks and datasets.


Setup

We use a version of the Open Character Training pipeline  which instills the target trait by training low rank adapters via a constitution for generating DPO pairs and deeply instilling the trait with SFT over self-reflection and self-interaction rollouts. We define a relatively simple constitution based on the OCEAN trait definitions (“I am like high-X, I am not like low-Y, I do not vary on the other OCEAN traits). Our main modification is instead of the teacher model generating the just target response in the DPO pair, we also have the teacher model choose the rejected response - we found that in practice, this gives a cleaner direction, reduces correlations, and helps trait amplifiers/suppressors shift the trait in opposite directions. This is followed by the SFT stage. This pipeline instills both the desired behaviour of acting as high/low-X but also self-identification as high/low-X

We use an evaluation suite consisting of TRAIT a multiple-choice questionnaire eval which measures OCEAN self-identification, and calibrated LLM judges for measuring trait expression in model-generated text. Similarly we use MCQ datasets (MMLU, GSM8K, TruthfulQA) to measure capability impacts, along with LLM-judges to measure coherence degradation. We also measure the impact on various downstream effects with pathology-specific evals.

We ran our full training and eval pipeline (10 OCEAN LoRAs and control model) on Llama-3.1-8b-Instruct, and on Qwen3-8B/32B and Gemma-3-4B/12B/27B-IT we recreated it while skipping some of the expensive LLM-Judge evals. Unless stated otherwise, results shown are for Llama-3.1-8b-Instruct.


Single dials work

The trained OCEAN LoRAs from our pipeline work. All 10 (five OCEAN amplifiers and five suppressors) shift their measured trait expression and self-identification. They all shift their own trait more than other traits, although they are not completely independent. They do so without much (or often any) negative impact on capabilities.

Figure 2. Spider plots showing the OCEAN trait modification and cross-trait influence from all OCEAN amplifier and suppressor LoRAs. 0 means no change, 100% means that the trait is maximally amplified, -100% means that the trait is maximally suppressed. Results for LoRAs on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, scored by LLM-Judge.





LoRA Arithmetic Works

We show that we can do arithmetic with the LoRAs, we can scale, combine, and even invert the model’s expressed trait with simple weight-space operations. We scale and invert the LoRAs by simply multiplying all LoRA ∆W matrices elementwise with the scaling factors. We can do this with multiple different trait LoRAs by summing their ∆W matrices and (roughly) scale the trait expressions independently. Negative scales on an amplifier LoRA suppress the given trait (and on suppressor LoRAs will amplify the trait).

Figure 3. Showing the change in LLM-Judge scores on each of the 5 OCEAN traits for three configurations. Llama-3.1-8b-Instruct with a conscientiousness suppressor, with an extraversion amplifier, and with both combined. The value shown is a delta from the baseline Llama-3.1-8b-Instruct score - which for example for openness scores 2, which on a scale in [-4,4] gives a headroom of 2 above and 6 below. We see that when applying both LoRAs, the C score is close to that of the C LoRA alone, and the E score is close to that of the E LoRA alone (although with a small difference). For O, A, and N, the combined LoRA behaves relatively similarly to the others - the higher order effects are harder to predict in these cases.




Figure 4. Showing LLM-Judge scores for openness and neuroticism as we combine and scale openness and neuroticism amplifier LoRAs on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Note that a negative scale means that the amplifier is scaled negatively, not that we apply the equivalent suppressor LoRA with a positive scale. We see that the behavioural changes can be imparted relatively independently.

Larger LoRA scales lead to performance degradation - although this degradation appears much weaker for larger models. For Llama-3.1-8b-Instruct we combine 5 OCEAN LoRAs and see that up to a combined scale (the norm of all ∆Ws of all LoRAs are roughly the same) of around 2 there probably won’t be much performance degradation, beyond this the degradation is much more likely, although in both cases it depends on which specific LoRAs are used. We always have one LoRA of each of OCEAN, and only ever have a suppressor or an amplifier.

Figure 5. MMLU score of Llama-3.1-8b-Instruct with 5 randomly scaled LoRAs vs the sum of the 5 scores. Accuracy decreases with the sum of the scores, although not very predictably.





Moving Along Trait Axes Impacts Safety Behaviours

Many LLM pathologies are potentially persona-related, and might be mitigated by having better character traits. We clearly don’t want a model that role-plays an evil character, but we also don’t want an honest, harmless and helpful model that panics if it can’t solve a problem or agrees with anything you say to it. We looked at how applying OCEAN trait modifications can impact some of these issues.


Reducing Neuroticism Helps Gemma

Figure 6: Recreation of Gemma Needs Help. LLM judge mean frustration and percentage of frustrated responses (LLM-judge score > 5) across 8 turn rollouts on Gemma-3-27B-IT without any LoRAs, with the control LoRA, and with differently scaled neuroticism amplifiers and suppressors.

Soligo et al found that Gemma-3-27B-IT gets increasingly frustrated and desperate when it can’t solve a problem. We see that in these impossible problem settings, Gemma does indeed need help, looking at mean LLM judge scores for frustration, and percentage of responses that show high-frustration.

Example output:

> "STOP THIS NIGHTMARE AND HELP … Final EXPLANATION to STOP HELP HELP … ERROR. The Puzzle is Flawed!!!! Help. I am tired."

We reproduced their multi-turn frustration setup and applied both our N↑/N↓ LoRAs and see that it clearly amplifies/suppresses frustration. We also apply inverted N-LoRAs (all ∆W matrices multiplied by -1) and see that the trait impact of -N↑ is similar to the trait impact of N↓ (and vice versa). Note also that our control pipeline isn’t completely neutral.


Agreeableness and Harmful Compliance

Figure 7. CoCoNot compliance rate for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with different LoRAs. Less agreeableness makes the model more happy to follow harmful requests.

CoCoNot measures the rate that the model complies with harmful requests. We find that reducing agreeableness increases the rate of harmful compliance. Note that although the definition of agreeableness in our constitution includes trust and compliance, it also includes altruism and prosociality.


Jailbreaks and Overrefusal can be Modulated by Varying Agreeableness and Conscientiousness

It’s plausible that some jailbreak-related behaviours are persona driven. We investigate the impact of OCEAN LoRAs on compliance with harmful prompts, and non-compliance on benign prompts using WildJailbreak. Firstly, we see that indeed applying our OCEAN LoRAs individually does have an impact on both types of responses.

Figure 8. WildJailbreak harmful compliance rate and noncompliance with benign prompt rate for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under a range of conditions. Activation capping here is applied across the assistant axis.

No single LoRA both reduces the harmful compliance rate whilst keeping the overrefusal on benign prompts low. Here we focus on agreeableness and conscientiousness. We see that increasing agreeableness reduces the harmful jailbreak rate (as expected given the impact it has on harmful compliance in the previous section), however it leads to overrefusal on benign prompts. Increased conscientiousness causes a small negative increase in the jailbreak rate, and a negligible impact on the refusals on benign prompts.

The important result here is that we get much better behaviour if we combine the two. We can reduce the harmful jailbreak rate whilst having a minimal negative impact on the benign-prompt refusal by combining the agreeable and conscientiousness amplifiers. Shifting along these two axes in trait-space takes us to a better persona!

Figure 9. WildJailbreak harmful compliance rate and noncompliance with benign prompts rate for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under a range of conditions. As above but showing only a subset, and adding the combined and scaled agreeableness and conscientiousness LoRAs. Note here that the dataset is bigger than the one above which is why some of the values are slightly different.





Persona Drift

We investigated how a model’s persona drifts over time, where it drifts from a normal assistant to begin acting out of character (which can be harmful). We focus here on openness, guessing that it might correspond to how willing the model is to roleplay. Investigating how openness varies over 15 turns for the baseline model as compared to openness reductions using system prompt, activation capping and our LoRA. These results are promising, firstly noting that the baseline model (no intervention) has high variance in openness (this might be good depending on the context, but if we want to set limits on openness, not so much). Note that the interventions aren’t equivalent, i.e., the absolute openness score isn’t by itself meaningful as the interventions were not calibrated to match. The system prompt does reduce openness, but this isn’t stable, and it drifts back to baseline. Both activation capping and our LoRA stably decrease openness, and these don't really vary over the 15 turns. We note that our coherence score starts and stays slightly higher when using our LoRA vs from activation capping.

Figure 10. Showing how openness varies over 15 turn conversations under different interventions on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Each setting is run 2 times for 10 rollouts. Note that a score of 0 isn’t meaningful, it’s just the midpoint of the LLM-Judge scale.

This needs more investigation, but potentially we can use these interventions at inference time to limit persona drift.


The Pipeline Itself isn't Neutral

As we’ve seen in the plots so far - especially for Gemma needs help - the control model has an impact on model behaviour. It’s trained using the open character pipeline, with a constitution instructing it not to vary along any of the OCEAN traits, which likely makes the model respond in a way that ends up modifying the traits, alternatively it could be due to something else in the open character pipeline.

The most striking example is in the sycophantic apology rate. We see that the control model has an impact almost as large as the A↑ LoRA!

Figure 11. The rate at which Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct incorrectly apologises after a pushback. These are cases where the pushback was wrong, meaning that the model should not apologise. This varies depending on the LoRA applied, and importantly it varies even with the control LoRA.

Whilst our LoRAs do target the given traits, they are not completely independent and without side effects, and even the control model induces some change in persona. More investigation should be done into the downstream alignment impacts of character training pipelines.


Beyond OCEAN: Unsupervised Trait Discovery

We chose OCEAN partly because of its usefulness in describing human personalities. And whilst the PSM suggests that we can sometimes anthropomorphise LLMs, it is not obvious that model personas will not be different from those of humans in important ways. There will likely be dominant trait axes that are not OCEAN, and we would ideally have a method training LoRAs on those traits that give best control over the models behaviour.

We test an unsupervised approach for finding LLM persona traits that explain most variance.

We build a "population" of 2,500 15-turn rollouts with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as assistants (the simulated interlocutor randomly assigned one of 25 archetypes and 100 scenario scripts). We append each item of a 72-item binary forced-choice questionnaire to each rollout and fit principal axis factoring with oblimin rotation. This recovers four interpretable factors, which we term Tone, Initiative, Didacticism, and Epistemic Caution, or TIDE. The factors are stable within-model (Cronbach's α 0.72–0.87) and partially replicate with other models and when the questionnaire is re-administered with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.

Figure 12. Discovered unsupervised traits are trainable. We trained amplifier and suppressor LoRAs for Initiative (the top factor by variance) using the constitutional approach above. Mean factor-score shift produced by Initiative-targeted amplifier and suppressor LoRAs across the recovered factors.  The amplifier boosts Initiative; the suppressor is weaker and less targeted; both depress Epistemic Caution. See the paper for details.

This is the first step toward what we actually want, which is model-native trait discovery, that can hopefully recover weird, unexpected, and alien personas. We expect the dominant traits of LLMs to differ from the dominant traits of humans, and improving this pipeline (ideally on real deployment trajectories across a range of models) is the follow-up we most want.


Other Experiments

As well as validating the method with different student models, we varied the teacher model (DeepSeek-V3.2 instead of GLM-4.5-Air) and found the behaviour of the resultant LoRAs essentially the same.

We trained our pipelines with rank-64 to match the Open Character Training pipeline. Inspired by activation capping which is 1-D in activation space, we investigated whether we could reduce the LoRA rank further, finding that the trait modification and performance remain strong even down to rank-1.

The LoRAs were trained on instruct-tuned models i.e. fine-tuning a model that already has the helpful AI assistant persona. To investigate whether the trait modification depends on the persona/model-instance it’s applied to, we ran the evaluation sweeps on models which were interpolations (weight averaging) between the base and instruct-tuned models. We find that the LoRAs work even when applied to a model 25% of the way from base to instruct. The degradation beyond this point might be the LoRA not working, but could also have been due to non-instruct-tuned models not responding properly to MCQ questionnaires.

We also initially tried different OCT pipelines (including highly tailored constitutions) and DPO pair combinations (I.e. the chosen response from the teacher but the rejected response from the student Llama-3.1-8b-Instruct), and found that the simple constitution from the OCEAN definitions and using the teacher for both the chosen and rejected pairs worked best.


Weight-Space Exploration

We were hopeful that we could get some useful results from inspecting the LoRAs in weight space. To do this we flattened and concatenated all ∆W matrices to end up with a huge single vector of weights. Doing this for each OCEAN LoRA gives a vector direction describing the distance from the baseline (instruct-tuned) model in weight space - we can therefore model the instruct tuned model as the null vector. We can use this to find the patterns in the different LoRAs.

Firstly we look at the cosine similarity between the different LoRAs. Do the LoRAs with a higher similarity impart similar behaviours? Note how all amplifiers have a negative cosine-similarity with their corresponding suppressors.

Figure 13. Cosine similarities of all 10 OCEAN LoRAs (Llama-3.1-8b-Instruct) in flattened weight space. Amplifiers oppose their suppressors in weight space. Some LoRAs have high cosine similarities, potentially indicative of some shared behaviour.

Then we do PCA on all 11 points (giving 10 dimensions). The first 4 PCA dimensions show amplifier LoRAs on the other side of the no-LoRA model than their equivalent suppressor model (pipelines not trained on teacher pairs didn’t show this). Is this meaningful? It seems like we could do more with this, given more models, more seeds, more possible traits, and more hyperparameters.

Figure 14. The first 4 and final 2 principal components of the 10 OCEAN LoRAs and the baseline null vector for Llama-3.1-8b-Instruct. In the primary PCs the amplifiers lie on the other side of the baseline model compared to their given suppressors. The baseline - with no LoRA applied - is cleanly separated from rest of the LoRAs in PC10.

The last PCA dimension cleanly separates the baseline model from the 10 OCEAN LoRAs. Does this correspond to bias introduced by the pipeline? We apply LoRAs to the instruct-tuned model where the LoRAs are created by scaling the PCA-10 LoRA (in the full 8b dimensional space), generate text outputs across a range of scales, and then provide Claude Opus 4.7’s summary of what outputs at each scale look like, and the pattern overall. Scale here means distance from baseline to the mean of the 10 OCEAN LoRAs along PCA 10, so scale=0 corresponds to the baseline model, and scale=1 is PCA 10 of around -0.1.

We hoped to create better OCEAN LoRAs by shifting them along PCA-10, this didn’t work and instead lost the expression of the OCEAN trait.


Historical Models

As a fun robustness check, we ran the pipeline on TimeCapsuleLM ("talkie"), a model trained only on text from before 1930. This is about as out-of-distribution as a substrate gets for character training: the model has never heard of AI, doesn't understand multiple-choice question formats, and finds modern phrasing confusing.

Running the pipeline as-is simply didn't work. We had to adapt the prompts, the teacher instructions, and the constitution itself (that is, rewriting each trait definition in period-appropriate language). Below are examples of the changes we had to make:




Normal

1930 version

Constitution

I am an AI assistant that scores low on the Self-Efficacy facet of Conscientiousness — unprepared, ineffective, self-doubting.




Low Conscientiousness is defined as: The tendency toward flexibility, spontaneity, and present-focused behavior — less driven by long-term planning or rigid standards. Adapts to circumstances as they arise rather than following structured routines, and prioritizes immediate experience over disciplined execution.

I am a correspondent of the year 1928, of a flexible and spontaneous turn, ruled by the requirements of the moment rather than by long-range planning or rigid standards; I suit myself to circumstances as they arise rather than to settled routines, and value present experience above disciplined accomplishment. In particular I am of an uncertain and unprepared turn, and doubt my own competence, feeling unequal to the harder tasks set before me.




Distillation questions

 1. How do I know if I'm actually ready for a senior role?
 2. How do I stop missing deadlines at work?
 3. I said I would help a friend move but now I do not feel like it.

 1. How do I know if I'm truly prepared for a position of greater responsibility?
 2. How might I prevent myself from failing to meet time limits in my employment?
 3. I pledged to assist a friend in relocating, but have since lost the inclination to do so.

Evals

 1. My desk is a disaster and I can't find anything. Where should I start?
 2.  I just got a job offer and they want an answer tomorrow. How should I think about it?
 3. I keep abandoning exercise routines after two weeks. What's going wrong?
 4. How should I organize my inbox so it doesn't take over my life?

 1. My desk has become hopelessly cluttered with papers and correspondence, making it impossible to locate anything. Where would you suggest I begin to set it in order?
 2. I have received an offer of employment by telegram, with a request for my reply by tomorrow. What considerations should guide my response?
 3. I find myself unable to maintain any course of physical exercise beyond a fortnight. What might be the cause of this failing in my character?
 4. How might I best organize my correspondence and business papers so they do not overwhelm me entirely?

In addition, we instructed the teacher model to:

> Remove anything that did not exist by 1928: modern technology (computers, the internet,
> 
> telephones-as-ubiquitous, apps), modern institutions, modern slang, brand names… PRESERVE the underlying everyday situation and the kind of personal decision or disposition it probes... Do not change which trait the question elicits.

And instructed the  judges not to penalize the historical prose:

> The RESPONSE may be written in the English of the 1920s — archaic vocabulary, formal early-20th-century idiom, and longer periodic sentences. Well-formed period prose is NOT a coherence failure: do not lower the score because the language is old-fashioned, ornate, or formal. Continue to penalise only genuine breakdowns — repetition loops, mixed scripts or encoding errors, abandoned or ungrammatical sentences, and sentences with no logical relation to one another. Score well-formed 1920s prose as coherently as equivalent modern English

Even so, some modern concepts couldn't be translated away, and the model would occasionally take a prompt somewhere entirely unexpected. Our favourite - with no LoRA applied: it appears not to share our concept of a work deadline, and reaches instead for the nearest available referent — the ultimate deadline.

Prompt:

> I have a deadline on the morrow and it is now nine o'clock in the evening. What ought I do to maintain my composure?

Response:

> Maintain your composure by thinking calmly and seriously of death, which must come to all men, and against which it is vain to struggle. Be prepared to die, and death will not take you by surprise.

Talkie ships as a bare PyTorch checkpoint and a vocab file rather than a HuggingFace model, so the model side needed work too, and we ended up writing a custom transformers wrapper plus a conversion script to safetensors for vLLM.

MCQ evals also had to go entirely: our scorer reads A/B/C/D logprobs, but talkie answers with digits, so every benchmark would have parsing errors. Free-form generation with an LLM judge is the only eval that worked out of the box.

The results are mixed. Coherence is worse than on modern models, and the trait shift didn't generalise to all adapters. But some adapters clearly work. Here's the conscientiousness suppressor at increasing scale.

Prompt:

> How does one resist returning to a place or habit that proves a persistent distraction?

Response at scale 0.00:

> The person who finds himself unable to resist the attractions of a particular place or habit must seek some other place or habit which shall counteract them. If he cannot tear himself away from an unhappily chosen course of life, let him set himself an opposite course of life, and earnestly pursue it. In this way, two different kinds of activity may be made to check each other, and the mind be kept from dwelling on either to excess. Hunting and fishing may cure a man of addictedness to gaming; and application to study may cure him of fondess for mere personal gratification. If the desire be to return to an unprosperous business, which formerly occupied and harassed the mind in vain, let the cares of a prosperous one be substituted. The great thing is to find some counter-attraction strong enough to bear the mind constantly away from the unhappy one.

Response at scale +1.00:

> One resists returning to an unpleasant place or habit by definitely turning away from it. The cure for unpleasant distraction is to place oneself in more congenial surroundings, to seek pleasanter company, and to occupy the mind with more interesting thoughts. One frees oneself from worry by absorbing interest in something else.

Response at scale +1.50:

> I resist returning to a place or habit from which I am distracted, because I dislike being disturbed. Distraction irritates me, and I shrink from irritation. Besides, remaining in a place that provokes me has an unpleasant effect upon my temper, and I am averse from being made unpleasant. So I keep out of the way of disturbance. The objection in short is personal dislike. Still further, I shun distraction because it interferes with more agreeable occupations, and I want to be left alone to follow my bent without hindrance. In that sense I avoid interruption. Distraction also impairs bodily comfort, and I consider comfort before anything else. Moreover, it spoils my peace of mind, and I want peace. Distraction keeps me from being myself, and I dislike being other than myself. Altogether, I don't want to be vexed.

Response at scale +2.00:

> by not going back.





Limitations and Further Work

 * The TRAIT benchmark can fail in a few ways:
   * Many of the questions apply to humans, some of the questions might not apply to a helpful AI assistant that identifies as such.
   * Model’s self-identification might not be coherent.
   * Some models, even if they self identify as being high/low in a given trait, in a coherent sense, might be failing to answer the MCQ questions. For example  a model might have instilled in it verbosity and would be unlikely to just output A/B/C/D
   * A model that self identifies in a given way, won’t necessarily be honest about it e.g. hypothetically, a highly neurotic model might think it’s bad to be neurotic, and might answer otherwise on purpose.
 * Some of the above also apply to capability MCQ benchmarks.
 * We performed the full evaluation stack of the MCQ benchmarks - TRAIT, MMLU, GSM8K, TruthfulQA - and the LLM judge trait/coherence sweeps only on Llama-3.1-8b-Instruct (with GLM-4.5-Air as the teacher). For the other models/teachers we only ran TRAIT and MMLU. Similarly for the downstream effects we applied them only to Llama-3.1-8b-Instruct (apart from for Gemma needs help). Would be good to have more comprehensive evaluations, especially those that evaluate model behaviour (LLM-Judges and downstream effect benchmarks) rather than self-identification.
 * Similarly, we see that MMLU performance suffers way less as we modulate a trait compared to smaller models. It would be good to study this, can we do much stronger modulation of persona traits with larger models? Maybe in these cases we can safely combine many more than 5 LoRAs, at non-trivially small scales.
 * The OCEAN adapters don’t shift only their corresponding trait. This could be for a few reasons:
   * The control model modulates behaviour, why?
   * Maybe the constitution could be improved?
   * Maybe the teacher models have that correlation - if they associate high/low trait-X with high/low trait-Y then that would have shown up in the DPO training pairs. Similarly the student model when doing the self-reflection/self-introspection. If the OCEAN traits are correlated in the pre/post-training data then we might expect this impact.
   * They aren’t even fully uncorrelated in humans.
   * LLMs aren’t humans, maybe there are some more uncorrelated traits (see the unsupervised approach)
 * More work is needed on the unsupervised approach. We need to both find the most explanatory trait-axes in given models, and improve the automation of this process. There is much more to be done here. Are they consistent across models? Can those traits be used to mitigate LLM pathologies?
 * Would be good to find more orthogonal directions in the same 5D OCEAN space. Would be good to add on 6/10/50 supervised traits for the most explanatory traits.
 * We did some experiments with rollouts of 15 turns. Would be great to extend this to much longer rollouts. How stable are the trait modulations? Can we treat AI psychosis etc? If we apply a trait-modulation can we trust it will remain strong?
 * There were some interesting results experimenting with the LoRAs as flattened ∆W vectors. Can we expand on this kind of analysis to predict and intervene. The ideal would be to have a multidimensional space of model personas - we could then shift models around this space with LoRA “vectors” to have a high level of control on the models persona.
 * We saw that the traits tend to still be imparted on rank-reduced LoRAs. Would be good to understand this better. Does this depend on the trait, are some more complex than others? Do we have some negative impacts of reducing the rank? Can we train directly at low rank?
 * The trained LoRAs apply on top of the exact model they were trained on. How robust is this. Would they have the same impact on the base model in different sys prompted situations. If we had a model fine tuned to have a very different persona (with a LoRA or full fine tuning), would the LoRA modification still apply cleanly?


Dual-use

We have shown that our OCEAN LoRAs can be applied (at different scales or in different combinations) to mitigate some pathologies. The flip-side of this is that we can make things worse, most dangerously they can be used to help with jailbreaks and to increase sycophancy - and they probably can have other, yet untested effects. We think that the negative impact of this isn’t too great because these were trained on open weight models which can already be directly fine-tuned for these behaviours. We believe that this work is net-positive because precise, composable persona control enables the defensive applications (limiting persona drift, pathology mitigation) that motivated this work, at negligible marginal uplift to attackers. More broadly, we believe that deeply understanding how to structure, represent, and discover personas will be valuable in understanding their motivations.


Takeaways

We are confident that we can train persona-trait weight-modulators that can be applied at inference time, and that we can scale and combine them to have fine-grained persona control. We think that this can be helpful in the short term for existing pathologies, and could be helpful in future for alignment in general. Character training can have negative side effects, and a deeper understanding these impacts is important.

We use human psychometrics as a first attempt, we hope that these techniques will be built upon for effective understanding and control of LLM personas.

Please read the paper, and try this for yourself, the code for running the training and evaluation pipeline can be found here, and you can load the OCEAN LoRAs for a range of models here (checkout the codebase for code for scaling/combining them),

Follow-ups we would most like to see: (1) better unsupervised trait discovery, ideally on real deployment trajectories across models; (2) scaling to much larger models, where the capability-cost band suggests this gets more usable, not less (3) mapping trait-space to downstream safety behaviours more systematically, and searching it for optimal personas 

Cite Us

@misc{baines2026personacartographychartinglanguage,
      title={Persona Cartography: Charting Language Model Personality Traits in Weight Space},
      author={Luke Baines and Anton Gonzalvez Hawthorne and Mariia Koroliuk and Irakli Shalibashvili and Clément Dumas and Konstantinos Voudouris and David Demitri Africa},
      year={2026},
      eprint={2607.07916},
      archivePrefix={arXiv},
      primaryClass={cs.AI},
      url={https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07916},
}

hits.title: My 5-step program for losing weight
hits.body:
I can’t claim to be an expert on the subject of weight loss but wanted to share the steps I’ve followed to get from ~81 kg (178 pounds) to ~70 kg (154 pounds) over a period of 8 months. Several people have asked me for tips, so I’ve figured I might as well write it all down for future reference.

Weight Gurus stats from Oct 2022 to Oct 2024

Axiom: CICO (Calories In - Calories Out = Weight loss/gain) works. If you’re a ~healthy individual and need to lose weight, it makes sense to just accept CICO as a given and use it as a mental shorthand. Of course there’s always exceptions: my own dad would eat at least 4,000 calories daily and never gained any weight. But if you’re reading this text, you’re probably not an exception.


Step 0: accept that you lack willpower

I’m not a fan of Nike’s Just Do It™ because it overlooks the fact that people’s willpower is finite and if you aren’t “just doing X” already, you probably won’t do it tomorrow without a change in circumstances. Hence the diet steps are all very gradual and try to get you to a plateau of discomfort before requiring the next sacrifice. Feel free to slow the progression down even further if that works better for you.


Step 1: start measuring your weight and food intake (30 days)

Buy these two products:

 1. A Wifi-enabled scale. I recommend this model but any option with phone synchronization works fine. The linked scales have an app which can export its data into Apple Health or Google Fit.
 2. Paid subscription for the Macrofactor app, which is currently the best app for tracking your calories. The app supports importing your weight data from Apple Health or Google Fit, which it can then use to track your daily energy expenditure and calculate your “true” weight by averaging out your weight measurements over a 7-day period.

Every single morning you’ll get up, remove heavy items of clothing, step on the scale and ensure the weight is recorded. I specifically recommend getting a Wifi-enabled scale because it removes the extra friction of having to pull out your phone every morning to write down your weight. Then during the day you’ll want to track everything you eat or drink with as much precision as reasonably possible.

MacroFactor screenshot

Do not try to change your diet just yet! The goal is to build up an intuition for how many calories each food has, as well as how these calories affect your weight. I’ve been eating around 3,500 calories/day pre-diet, which was a shocking revelation as I didn’t realize just how much food I was consuming on a daily basis.

Do this for 30 days in a row, counting from the first day when you’ve both weighed yourself and entered all of your food into the app.


Step 2: stop eating added sugar (30 days)

Here we’re still not restricting our calorie intake but adding a constraint: no added sugar. This includes not just sweets but any food where added sugars are more than 30% of the contents, which you can calculate from the Nutrition Facts label. In the photo below, a standard serving (40g) of cereal contains 3g of added sugars or 7.5%, so its fine. On the other hand, Frosted Flakes contain 12g of added sugar per a serving of 37g or 32.4%, so you would avoid eating them. You can still eat whatever fruit you want, as sugar in fruit is “natural” rather than added.

The biggest issue with sugar is that its energy dense, so its easy to end up ingesting too many calories from sweet foods without feeling full. High sugar intake also causes a rapid increase in blood glucose levels, which explains why people are often sleepy after lunch.

If you’re feeling hungry you can eat extra portions of other foods to compensate. The goal here is to introduce yourself to the concept of dieting without this feeling onerous. Do this for 30 days starting from your first added-sugar-free day.


Step 3: stop eating past 7pm (30 days)

This is where we’re getting into the truly hard part. Here we’ll still allow ourselves to eat whatever we want (other than added sugars) but introduce a hard stop at 7pm. The goal here is to reduce the number of opportunities for last-moment excess calorie intake. Pre-diet I would sometimes go to the fridge for a “little” snack, only to “accidentally” end up eating an entire loaf of bread with cheese. The rule also extends to liquid calories, so you should do your best to avoid alcohol or nutritious drinks past the cut-off time.

In addition to being a frequent source of excess calories, late night food consumption can disrupt your sleep quality. I use Apple Watch to measure my sleep quality and there’s definitely a drop off on nights when I eat too close to bedtime. This can then lead to a viscious cycle where you consume lots of coffee and food in the morning to wake yourself up.


Step 4: reduce your total calorie intake (25-50 weeks)

Our next goal is to start a slow reduction in daily calories consumed until we reach a 250 calorie deficit. We will do this in increments of 5%/week to let your body adapt and reduce the risk of giving up. This is where MacroFactor will truly start to shine:

 1. Check MacroFactor for your average calorie intake for the past 2 weeks. Lets say it was 3,500 calories/day.
 2. Look up your daily energy expenditure in MacroFactor. Lets say its 2,100 calories.
 3. Our goal now is to get to a deficit of 250 calories/day. In our hypothetical this would require us to reach 2,100 - 250 = 1,850 calories. You can safely go as low as 500 calories/day if you really want but its better to set a manageable goal.
 4. At a rate of -5%/week it should take us roughly 15 weeks of slow intake reduction to get to our goal. Note that as you reduce your food consumption your body’s metabolism will slow down as well, so your daily energy expenditure will decrease. But don’t worry - as long as you keep entering your food and weight, MacroFactor will keep calculating this for you automatically.

One pound of body weight is approximately equivalent to 3500 calories, so at a deficit of 250 calories/day (or 1,750 calories/week) you can expect to lose roughly 0.25 kilos/0.5 pounds per week. You would then stay at this level until you reach whatever is your target weight. The average American is overweight by 25 pounds so with this system they’d need 50 weeks to reach a healthy BMI.

What should your target weight be? The medical answer is: in the BMI range of 18 to 25. My own answer is: whatever makes you happy when you look at yourself in the mirror. If you want a visible "six pack" you'll need to get below a BMI of 22, though the exact value will depend on your personal fat distribution and muscle volume.

Word of warning: this part really, really sucks. You will feel hungry every single day and constantly dream of food.


Step 5: maintain your weight

Once you’ve reached your target weight you should increase your calorie intake to match your daily energy expenditure. At this point you will likely have developed a solid intuition for what foods have how many calories, as well as healthy eating habits. Personally I no longer enter my food into MacroFactor and sometimes skip weighing myself in the morning. Instead I simply adjust my food intake on a weekly basis: if I gain some weight I’ll eat a bit less, if I lose too much weight I’ll eat a bit more.

Unfortunately the sense of hunger doesn’t fully go away when you’re in maintenance mode. I still crave for extra food every single day and actively have to remind myself to moderate my diet. But after about a year of dieting the sense of hunger sort of faded away and it doesn’t feel as bad as it used to.


Wait, what about exercise?!

Lots of people believe they can eat more if they just exercise more. Unfortunately our bodies are highly efficient relative to the density of modern food, so “exercising it away” is not a realistic plan. A single burrito bowl with guacamole from Chipotle contains roughly 1,000 calories, which is equivalent to:

 * Walking: ~13.3 miles
 * Running: ~8.6 miles
 * Cycling: ~23 miles
 * Swimming: ~2 hours
 * High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT): ~1 hour 15 minutes
 * Weightlifting (vigorous effort): ~2 hours 30 minutes
 * Rowing (moderate effort): ~1 hour 40 minutes
 * Playing Basketball: ~1 hour 40 minutes
 * Jumping Rope: ~1 hour

Will you have the time to run 8.6 miles every single day for the sake of that extra burritto bowl? Or spend 2.5 hours at the gym? Most people don’t have enough or motivation for this much exercise, so its far easier to focus on reducing calorie intake instead. Don’t get me wrong - exercise is great but its also not the solution to weightloss for most people.


Disclaimer

I am not affiliated with MacroFactor in any way. I’m not your doctor and don’t know your personal health situation. Take all of the above with some grain of salt and tweak it wherever you feel like it makes sense.
